entries.title: Beginner (novice)
entries.take: A lifter who still progresses on a simple, repeated routine. The 2009 ACSM position stand uses novice for people with no lifting experience, or none for several years.

entries.title: A first programme looks much the same whatever the long-term goal
entries.take: Health, physique, sport and powerlifting beginners need the same base first. The goal starts to shape the plan at the intermediate stage.
entries.body: Lyle McDonald's position is that the first months do one job for everyone: learn the movements, add some muscle and strength across the whole body, let joints and tendons catch up, and form the habit of turning up. A 2026 American College of Sports Medicine overview of 137 systematic reviews fits that view. Resistance training improved strength, size, power and physical function against no exercise, and few details of the prescription changed the main results. He makes one exception: Olympic weightlifting, whose lifts need a coach from the first session.
do: Pick a simple whole-body plan and run it for months before you specialise.

entries.title: Start with the least training that still makes you progress
entries.take: If a small amount of training produces gains, extra work adds risk and uses up the room you will need later.
entries.body: McDonald's rule for all training is to get the most adaptation from the least work, and to add more only when progress stops. A beginner who starts on an advanced lifter's volume has nothing left to raise once gains slow, and carries more risk of injury and burnout in the meantime. A meta-analysis of 140 strength studies points the same way: untrained people gained most at a mean load of 60% of one-rep max, trained people at 80%, and the authors read this as support for raising the dose as training status rises. The pull toward doing more is strong because more looks as though it must work better.
do: Raise sets, days or load when progress stalls, and not because another routine looks more serious.

entries.title: Counting years in the gym as proof you are past the beginner stage
entries.take: Time served does not make a lifter intermediate. Stable technique, the ability to work hard and measurable gains do.
entries.body: McDonald's observation from two decades of coaching is that almost everyone rates themselves as more advanced than they are. A person can lift for two years, or twenty, and still have unstable technique, little capacity for hard effort, no added muscle and a disorganised routine. In his terms that person remains a beginner and progresses fastest on beginner training for a while. He adds that experienced lifters, like athletes in other sports, go back to basic work for short spells on purpose. A return to a simple plan is a normal part of training.
do: Judge your level by technique and progress, then choose the routine that fits it.

entries.title: You stop being a beginner when simple training stops producing gains
entries.take: Expect roughly 6 to 12 months of proper training before a beginner routine runs out, by McDonald's estimate.
entries.body: McDonald lists three signs: sound, repeatable technique on the main exercises, the capacity to finish a full 60 to 90 minute session without being flattened, and some visible muscle gain. His simplest test is that the beginner routine no longer moves strength or size. He keeps a new lifter on beginner training for at least 3 months and often 6, and puts the usual switch at 6 to 12 months of proper training. The 2009 ACSM position stand draws a similar line, describing intermediates as people with about 6 months of consistent training. Switching early gains nothing, because progress never comes this easily again.
do: Stay on the simple plan for as long as weights or reps keep rising from week to week.

entries.title: Time before a beginner routine runs out
entries.take: McDonald's estimate of when a beginner becomes an intermediate. The 2009 ACSM stand puts intermediates at about 6 months of consistent training.

entries.title: Tendons adapt more slowly than strength rises
entries.take: Strength can climb by almost a third in two months while tendon stiffness has not yet changed, so add load more slowly than strength allows.
entries.body: Eight people did knee-extension training for three months. Strength was up 29.6% after two months, but tendon stiffness and muscle size had not changed by then and rose only by the end. A meta-analysis of 27 studies with 264 participants found that tendons do stiffen with training, that the effect depends on high loading, and that programmes of 12 weeks or more tended to do more. McDonald's coaching reading is that beginners who go heavy or train often too early are the ones who pick up elbow and knee trouble, and that a joint injured once is easily injured again.
do: Add load in small steps for the first months, even when a bigger jump feels possible.
Hold the weight if a joint or tendon stays sore, and see a clinician if the pain persists.

entries.title: Work capacity
entries.take: The amount of training you can do and recover from. Beginners build it slowly. Leaving every session exhausted means the workload is ahead of it.

entries.title: The ability to work hard is learned in small steps
entries.take: New lifters stop long before real fatigue. Pushing a little past the point where you would normally stop resets that limit over time.
entries.body: A scoping review found that people left to choose their own weights picked an average of 53% of their one-rep max, which is light for most goals. McDonald describes the same pattern in beginners: they believe they are far more tired than they are, and they stop when a set first becomes uncomfortable. His method is gradual. Each time a lifter does slightly more than they thought they could, the ceiling moves, and over months this adds up to a level of effort they would not have believed at the start. A coach helps by telling real fatigue from giving up. None of this means wrecking yourself in a session.
do: Once technique is steady, take one set per exercise a rep or two past where you would usually stop.

entries.title: Signs you have outgrown a beginner programme
entries.take: Drawn from Lyle McDonald's criteria. Most of each group should be true before you change to an intermediate plan.

groups.name: Technique
items: Each main exercise looks the same from the first rep to the last
You can feel the muscles an exercise is meant to train
Weight has gone up for months without the movement changing

groups.name: Capacity
items: A full session of 60 to 90 minutes no longer leaves you drained
Joints and tendons are free of lingering soreness at current loads
You have trained two or three times a week for six months or more with few missed sessions

groups.name: Progress
items: You are visibly more muscular or measurably stronger than when you started
Weights and reps have not moved for two full weeks
A 10 to 20% step back and rebuild did not take you past your old best

entries.title: Training variables (loading parameters)
entries.take: The settings that define a programme: intensity (how heavy), volume (how many sets and reps), frequency (how often) and exercise choice. Rest between sets and speed of movement are often added.

entries.title: Beginners gain strength on loads as light as 60% of their max
entries.take: Untrained people gained the most strength at about 60% of one-rep max in a large meta-analysis, so there is no need to start heavy.
entries.body: A meta-analysis of 140 studies found a mean load of 60% of one-rep max (1RM) gave untrained people their largest strength gains, against 80% for trained people. The 2009 ACSM stand gives novices loads they could lift 8 to 12 times. McDonald's reasons for starting light: early gains come mainly from learning the movement, technique is easier to learn below heavy loads, and joints get time to adapt. He keeps an average beginner under about 80% of max, roughly an eight-rep limit, for the first month or two. Heavy loads matter more later: the 2026 ACSM stand found loads of 80% or more enhanced strength.
do: Start with a weight you could lift for well over the target reps, and add load while technique holds.

entries.title: Load that maximised strength gains in untrained people
entries.take: Mean training load with the largest strength effect in untrained people across 140 studies. Trained people needed 80%.

entries.title: One set per exercise is enough to start; build to two or three
entries.take: A single set gives a new lifter most of the early strength gain. Extra sets add practice and a little more, at the cost of time.
entries.body: McDonald starts beginners on one set per exercise and builds toward three over the first weeks. A session of 8 to 10 exercises done once each takes 20 to 30 minutes and still works. The later sets mainly add practice and work capacity, and they help only if fatigue does not spoil technique. Pooled evidence agrees that more is somewhat better: a meta-analysis of 9 studies found higher weekly set volumes gave greater strength gains than low ones (effect size 0.18), and the 2026 ACSM stand found 2 to 3 sets enhanced strength. For basic fitness, he considers one hard set per exercise enough indefinitely.
do: Do one set per exercise in the first sessions.
Add a second and third set over the following weeks if you want more than basic fitness.

entries.title: Sets of 8 to 12 suit most beginners; sets of 5 need restraint
entries.take: Moderate reps keep the weight modest and give plenty of practice. Low reps work when someone stops you loading the bar too fast.
entries.body: The 2009 ACSM stand gives novices loads they can lift 8 to 12 times, and McDonald used the same range with his beginners. He explains the trade-offs. Very high reps bring fatigue that breaks technique late in the set, and a burn that puts new lifters off. Sets of 5 are short enough to keep every rep clean, but uncoached lifters tend to add weight faster than their technique or joints can follow. For most people he advises 8 to 12 reps for one to three sets, with three to five sets of 5 as an option for lifters who have a coach or real self-control.
do: Use 8 to 12 reps unless a coach is watching your lifts.

entries.title: Train the whole body two or three times a week at first
entries.take: Three weekly sessions gave untrained people the largest strength gains in one meta-analysis. Two is close and easier to schedule.
entries.body: A meta-analysis of 140 studies found untrained people gained most strength training each muscle group 3 days a week, and trained people 2 days. The 2009 ACSM stand recommends 2 to 3 days a week for novices. A later meta-analysis found frequency had no significant effect on strength once weekly volume was matched, so the gain from a third day probably comes from the extra practice and work. Two sessions can be moved around a busy week, while three need alternate days. McDonald regards two as enough indefinitely for general fitness, and three as close to required for anyone whose sport is lifting.
do: Choose two or three non-consecutive days you can keep every week.
Repeat the same exercises each session so every lift is practised often.

entries.title: Share of the three-day result from two sessions a week
entries.take: McDonald's estimate for beginners training twice a week instead of three times. A coaching figure, not a pooled result.

entries.title: Starting on a one-muscle-a-day bodybuilding split
entries.take: A split trains each exercise about once a week, which starves a beginner of practice and invites far more sets than needed.
entries.body: When weekly sets are matched, split and full-body routines produce similar strength and size in trials, so a split is not harmful in itself. McDonald's objection is specific to beginners. Each exercise comes round about once in seven days, so the movements are learned slowly. And because each session covers only one or two muscles, new lifters fill the time with exercises and sets they do not need. The only split he accepts for a beginner is upper body and lower body on separate days, used because it allows training two days in a row, and only with the sets for each muscle held down.
do: Use full-body sessions for the first months.
If your week forces a split, use upper and lower days and keep sets per muscle low.

entries.title: How a beginner plan shifts with the long-term goal
entries.take: The base is shared. These are the adjustments Lyle McDonald describes for each aim, arranged here as a comparison.
rows: Machines or any simple mix that can be learned in a session or two
1 set of 8 to 12 can be enough if it is worked hard
General whole-body lifts; bring in early any lift needed later
Free weights, machines and single-joint work; test which exercises suit your build
Build to 2 or 3 sets of 8 to 12
Squat, bench press and deadlift from the start, plus general work for the whole body
Sets of 5 on the main lifts for clean practice; 8 to 12 elsewhere
Both competition lifts need a coach from the first session

entries.title: Free weights and machines build similar strength and size
entries.take: A meta-analysis found no difference in muscle growth, and strength rose most on whichever equipment people had trained with.
entries.body: Thirteen studies with 1,016 participants compared the two for at least six weeks. Muscle growth, jump height and strength compared across test types did not differ. Strength tested with free weights rose more after free-weight training, and machine-tested strength tended to rise more after machine training, so the gain is specific to the tool. The 2026 ACSM stand also found that equipment type did not consistently change outcomes. The authors of the meta-analysis conclude that the choice comes down to preference and goals. A lifter who will be tested on a barbell lift has to train that lift.
do: Choose the equipment you can use well and consistently.
If a barbell lift is your test, train it with a barbell.

entries.title: Free weights and machines: the practical differences
entries.take: Results are similar, so the choice turns on practical points. These are the ones McDonald weighs for a new lifter.
rows: A barbell squat, bench press or deadlift can take weeks or months to learn well
Most can be learned in one or two sessions
You set the path, so it can fit your build
Fixed by the machine; a poor fit can strain a joint
Trained by the lift; a barrier for people with balance problems
Largely removed, so effort goes to the target muscle
A 20 kg (45 lb) plate weighs the same everywhere
Stacks and leverage differ by brand, so numbers do not transfer
A bar, plates, bench and rack cover dozens of exercises
Usually one machine per movement; no problem in a commercial gym
Plates to load and more warm-up sets
Set the seat and move the pin

entries.title: Compound and isolation exercises
entries.take: A compound (multi-joint) exercise moves two or more joints and works several muscles, as in a squat or row. An isolation (single-joint) exercise moves one joint, as in a leg extension or curl. Both exist as free-weight and machine versions.

entries.title: Multi-joint lifts save time; single-joint lifts fill the gaps
entries.take: With total work matched, multi-joint training gave larger strength gains than single-joint training and the same change in body composition.
entries.body: Thirty-six active men trained three times a week for eight weeks using only multi-joint or only single-joint exercises, with total work matched. Fat-free mass rose equally. The multi-joint group gained more one-rep-max strength (squat 13.8% against 8.3%, bench press 10.9% against 8.1%) and more aerobic capacity. McDonald's practical point is efficiency: one lower-body lift, one push, one pull and a trunk exercise cover most of the body. He keeps single-joint work for muscles that a compound lift trains poorly in a given person, and for the biceps, which have no true compound exercise.
do: Build each session around a lower-body lift, a push and a pull.
Add single-joint work where the big lifts leave a muscle undertrained.

entries.title: A machine circuit is a sound first programme
entries.take: For an untrained adult who wants general fitness, simple machines taught over a few sessions do the job with little to learn.
entries.body: McDonald started most beginner clients, mainly untrained adults over 30, on machines. He added exercises across the first three sessions, used one easy set of 8 to 12 on each, and added weight once 12 came easily. His reasoning: a leg press or machine chest press is safe after a session or two of teaching, and squatting or benching with a barbell is not. After six to eight weeks he brought in free-weight or more complex exercises on one day of the week, while the familiar ones carried the hard work on the other days. Trials showing machines and free weights build similar size support the approach.
do: Learn a few machine exercises first if nobody is available to teach you barbell lifts.
Introduce new exercises a few at a time after six to eight weeks.

entries.title: Keep the same exercises for the first six to eight weeks
entries.take: A new movement needs weeks of practice before you can load it or judge it, so early variety slows learning.
entries.body: McDonald prefers a beginner to repeat one set of exercises at every session, because frequent practice of the same movements is the quickest way through the early learning phase. Plans that alternate two different workouts halve the practice each lift gets. He holds a set of exercises for about six to eight weeks before trialling others, so that each movement gets a fair test. To judge whether an exercise suits a person he uses three signs: which muscle is felt working, where the pump appears, and where soreness shows up the next day. He calls all three imperfect but worth noting.
do: Run one set of exercises for six to eight weeks before swapping any.
Give each new exercise several weeks before you judge it.

entries.title: Find first weights by starting with the lightest option available
entries.take: Begin with the empty bar, the empty sled or the first plate on the stack, and add weight in later sets or sessions.
entries.body: McDonald's rule is to err light. Too little weight costs nothing, and too much can injure a new lifter or leave them too sore to come back. The first sessions are for technique, breathing and a steady speed, and nobody can attend to those under a load that scares them. He notes one catch: a weight can be so light that the lifter cannot feel the movement, so finding the right load may take two or three weeks. Starting points differ widely. A 20 kg (45 lb) bar suits most young men on the bench press, while many women begin with a dumbbell of about 2.5 kg (5 lb) in each hand.
do: Start each new exercise with the lightest load the equipment allows.
Add a little each set or session until you can feel the target muscles working.

entries.title: Setting first weights from a body-weight formula
entries.take: Rules that tell a beginner to squat or press a fixed share of body weight fit some people and badly overload others.
entries.body: Some programmes give starting loads as a fraction of body weight. McDonald rejects the idea for beginners and for everyone else. Two people of the same weight can differ in age, sex, build, training history and how much of that weight is muscle, so one ratio cannot suit both. A heavy, untrained 55-year-old and a light 20-year-old athlete would each get the wrong answer, in opposite directions. Even where a ratio matches the average new lifter, an individual has no way of knowing whether they are that average. Trial from the light end takes a session or two longer and carries none of that risk.
do: Ignore starting-weight ratios and work up from the lightest load.

entries.title: Use a rep range and add weight when you reach the top of it
entries.take: Work in a range such as 8 to 12. When the top number arrives in good form, add a little weight and build the reps back up.
entries.body: The usual name is double progression: reps rise first, then weight. McDonald uses it with beginners doing one work set. When 12 clean reps arrive and the final two are not a grind, the load goes up slightly, reps fall to 8 or 9, and the climb starts again. The 2009 ACSM stand gives a similar rule: raise the load by 2 to 10% once you can do one to two reps more than the target. In 39 previously untrained people followed for 10 weeks, progressing by adding reps or by adding load gave the same gains in strength and muscle size, so the exact method matters less than having one.
do: Pick a rep range for each exercise and log every set.
Add the smallest available weight when you reach the top of the range with clean reps.

entries.title: Load increase once you beat the rep target
entries.take: The 2009 ACSM stand's step size, applied when you can do one to two reps more than the target number.

entries.title: Judge a weight jump as a percentage of what is on the bar
entries.take: The same plate is a small step on a heavy lift and a huge one on a light lift, which hits smaller lifters and small exercises hardest.
entries.body: Going from 9 kg to 11.3 kg (20 to 25 lb) on a bench press is a 25% increase, far outside the 2 to 10% that the 2009 ACSM stand suggests, and it can turn ten good reps into none. McDonald points out that women meet this problem on many exercises, and that older machines with large stack increments cause it for everyone. A squat can usually take a 5 kg (10 lb) jump where a curl needs 1 to 2.5 kg (2.5 to 5 lb). His preference is always the smaller step, on the reasoning that a slow climb with intact technique ends up further ahead after three months than a fast one interrupted by injury.
do: Work out the next jump as a percentage before you load it.
Use the smallest plates, or add reps first, when the jump would exceed about 10%.

entries.title: Adding weight every session whether or not the last one was clean
entries.take: Plans that ask for more weight each time work when a coach makes the call. Alone, lifters keep adding after technique has begun to slip.
entries.body: Low-rep beginner plans usually ramp to one top set and ask for a small increase next time. McDonald accepts that beginners can ride this for a long while. His concern is the uncoached lifter, often a young man, who treats the increase as automatic. His own mentor's rule was stricter: add nothing until every set is completed under control, even if that means the same weights for the first month, and after that expect to add about once a week. McDonald sits between the two. He adds small amounts until the lifter can feel the lift, holds there until technique is stable, then progresses gradually.
do: Add weight only when every set at the current load was done under control.
Film a set or ask an experienced lifter to watch before raising the load.

entries.title: Back-cycle (reset)
entries.take: A planned step back after a stall: cut the load by 10 to 20%, then build up again over three to four weeks and aim to pass the old best.

entries.title: After two weeks without progress, drop the load and build back up
entries.take: A stall means about two full weeks with no gain in weight or reps. The standard answer is a 10 to 20% step back and a steady rebuild.
entries.body: McDonald expects a well-fed beginner on a simple plan to progress for three or four months before the first real stall. The two-week definition rules out reacting to a single bad day. The usual fix is to cut the load by 10 to 20% and climb again. Someone stuck at 85 kg (185 lb) for sets of five would restart at roughly 65 to 75 kg (145 to 165 lb) and should be back at the old weight, and able to pass it, within three to four weeks. The lighter weeks also let technique settle. He suggests repeated resets can carry a beginner through a first year. This is coaching practice, untested in trials.
do: Call a stall only after two weeks without a gain in weight or reps.
Cut the load 10 to 20% and rebuild over three to four weeks.

entries.title: Step back after a stall
entries.take: The reset McDonald describes after two weeks without progress, followed by a rebuild over three to four weeks.

entries.title: The usual next step is more sets, spread over upper and lower days
entries.take: When simple training stops working, most lifters need more weekly work, and splitting the body in two keeps sessions a sensible length.
entries.body: McDonald's test for moving on is a failed reset: you step the weights back, rebuild, and cannot pass your old best. For lifters who want more size or strength, the common change is higher volume. Full-body sessions then run too long, so he moves people to upper-body and lower-body days, each done twice a week. Sets for a muscle in one session rise from about 3 to about 6 and later 8, usually split between one compound and one single-joint exercise. The 2009 ACSM stand likewise lists 3 to 4 days a week for intermediates. Someone training for health can stay on the beginner plan and maintain.
do: Move on only after a reset and rebuild fails to beat your previous best.
Raise weekly sets in steps before changing anything else.

entries.title: Double progression
entries.take: A way of progressing inside a rep range such as 6 to 12: add reps from session to session until you reach the top of the range, then add weight, which drops you back toward the bottom, and build up again.

entries.title: Maximal strength
entries.take: The greatest force you can produce in one effort with no time limit. In the gym it is measured as a one-rep max. Coaches outside the lifting sports often track a 3- or 5-rep max to avoid true maximum attempts.

entries.title: Relative strength
entries.take: Strength divided by body weight. It matters most where you move your own body or compete in a weight class. Gaining weight faster than strength lowers it.

entries.title: Strength is muscle size multiplied by how well the nervous system uses it
entries.take: Bigger muscle raises the ceiling for strength. Skill, coordination and leverage decide how much of that ceiling you reach.
entries.body: Reviews attribute strength to morphological factors, chiefly muscle cross-sectional area, and to neural ones: motor unit recruitment, firing rate, coordination between muscles and reduced inhibition. Limb lengths and tendon attachment points also matter and cannot be trained. McDonald writes this as force equals muscular factors times neural factors, which explains a common puzzle: a smaller lifter with good leverage and years of practice in a lift can out-lift a bigger one. Heavy low-rep work is often called neural training because it mainly improves the second term, though enough sets of it still build muscle.
do: To lift more, build muscle and also practise the specific lift under heavy loads.

entries.title: Maximal strength work means heavy loads, few reps and long rests
entries.take: The 2026 ACSM stand found strength was enhanced by loads of 80% of max or more. Convention puts dedicated strength work at 85% and up for 1 to 5 reps.
entries.body: The 2026 ACSM overview of 137 reviews found voluntary strength was enhanced by loads of at least 80% of one-rep max, 2 to 3 sets, a full range of motion, doing the lift early in the session, and two or more weekly sessions. McDonald describes the classic maximal strength zone as 85 to 100% for about 1 to 5 reps, and stresses that the boundary is soft: loads of 75 to 85% also build strength, especially when the bar is moved as fast as possible. Rests run long: a review of strength training for athletes found 2 to 5 minutes between sets may give the greatest strength and power benefit.
do: Put the lift you most want to strengthen first in the session.
Rest 2 to 5 minutes between heavy sets.

entries.title: Dose that maximised strength gains, by training status
entries.take: Mean values from two meta-analyses and the 2026 ACSM overview. The older analyses counted sets that were mostly taken near a repetition maximum.

entries.title: Not everyone needs true maximal strength training
entries.take: Lifting sports and weight-class athletes need it most. For physique goals it is occasional, and for general health sets of 5 to 8 are heavy enough.
entries.body: McDonald sorts the need by goal. Powerlifters and weightlifters are judged on a one-rep max, and athletes in weight classes want strength without added mass. Other power athletes need it as a base. For physique training he sees it as an occasional tool, a few weeks every two or three months, because a higher max lets a lifter use more weight in growth rep ranges. For people training for health he would rarely go below about 5 reps unless a coach is present, since low-rep work is unforgiving of loose technique. Sets of 5 to 8 reach the 80% of max that the 2026 ACSM stand found enhanced strength.
do: Decide from your goal whether sets of 1 to 3 belong in your plan at all.

entries.title: For most sports, strength is a base to build and then maintain
entries.take: Stronger athletes sprint, jump and change direction better, but most sport actions last 0.1 to 0.2 seconds, too short to use maximal strength.
entries.body: One review concluded that greater strength is strongly associated with better jumping, sprinting and change of direction, and may have no substitute. A companion review advises weaker athletes to build strength first, and stronger ones to shift toward power. McDonald's version is that once strength is adequate, pushing gym numbers higher does little for performance, because sport gives so little time to apply force. He cites coaching targets of about 1.5 times body weight in the bench press and 2 times in the squat as the point where emphasis moves. These are conventions, untested.
do: If you are weak for your sport, get stronger first.
Once strong, hold strength with less work and spend the time on power and the sport itself.

entries.title: Grinding lifts cost more recovery than lifts that are made or missed quickly
entries.take: A rep fought through for several seconds taxes muscle, joints and nervous system far more than a fast lift, which limits how often it can be done.
entries.body: McDonald contrasts the two barbell sports. An Olympic lift is limited by speed, so a missed attempt simply does not go, and the lifts are technical enough to need near-daily practice. Powerlifts can be ground out over several seconds, and lifters have to practise that, but he judges such reps far more costly. His reading of high-frequency strength systems is that most of their work sits at about 75 to 85% of max, little is above 90% and almost none goes to failure. Truly heavy days still number about two a week for a lift, which matches the two days found best for trained people in a meta-analysis of 140 studies.
do: Count your truly heavy, slow sessions for a lift and keep them to about two a week.
Add extra practice of a lift only as lighter, faster sets.

entries.title: Prilepin's chart
entries.take: A table from Soviet weightlifting, attributed to A. S. Prilepin, that gives reps per set and total reps in a session for each band of intensity. It records what elite weightlifters did and was never tested in an experiment.

entries.title: Prilepin's chart describes elite weightlifters, so its upper volumes are too high for most
entries.take: The chart's logic is sound: keep reps per set well under the most you could do, and cut total reps as the load rises. Its numbers come from a narrow group.
entries.body: The chart's principle is that sets stop well short of the reps the load would allow, so bar speed and technique stay high, and that total reps in a session shrink as the weight climbs. McDonald lists its limits. It was observation, not an experiment. The lifters were elite young men training full time in a state system, very probably with anabolic drugs. It says nothing about how often they trained, and it was built for fast lifts. He advises ordinary lifters to use the lower to middle part of its ranges. The powerlifting coach Louie Simmons roughly halved its totals for the slower powerlifts.
do: Use the chart's low to middle volumes if you follow it at all.
Keep the principle: several crisp sets instead of one set to the limit.

entries.title: Heavy reps per exercise in a strength session
entries.take: From the old rule of 3 to 5 sets of 3 to 5 reps, which McDonald endorses for strength work. Stay low nearer 90% of max, higher nearer 85%.

entries.title: Programming five heavy sets of five on every exercise
entries.take: Heavy low-rep sets need rests of several minutes, so more than one or two such lifts makes a session unworkably long.
entries.body: Five sets of five with a three-minute rest take at least 15 minutes for one exercise before warm-up sets are counted. Two or three lifts done that way fill 45 to 60 minutes. McDonald's rule for strength phases is to train one or two main lifts heavy in a session and everything after them with lighter loads and higher reps. He also keeps very low reps for multi-joint lifts, because singles to triples on a single-joint exercise load one joint heavily for little return. A review of rest intervals found that 3 to 5 minutes between sets allowed more reps across sets at loads of 50 to 90% of max.
do: Pick one or two lifts to train heavy in a session.
Do the rest of the session at 8 or more reps with shorter rests.

entries.title: Power (muscular power)
entries.take: Work divided by the time taken to do it, or force multiplied by speed. Lifting the same weight through the same distance in half the time doubles the power.

entries.title: Rate of force development (RFD)
entries.take: How quickly force rises at the start of an effort. Sprint steps, jumps and throws allow only about 0.1 to 0.2 seconds, so the force you can reach in that window matters more than your slow maximum.

entries.title: Force-velocity curve
entries.take: The trade-off between the force a muscle can produce and its shortening speed: the faster the movement, the lower the force. Power, the product of the two, peaks in the middle of the curve.

entries.title: Kinds of training along the force-velocity curve
entries.take: From heavy and slow to light and fast. Loads are from the cited reviews; the sorting of sports follows Lyle McDonald's discussion.
rows: Powerlifting; linemen; a base for all power sports
Shot put, rugby and football forwards, sprint starts
Fast squats and presses, kettlebell swings
Body weight or a light implement
Top-speed sprinting; racket and bat speed

entries.title: Load that gave the highest power output, by exercise
entries.take: From two meta-analyses that sorted loads into three zones. The best load for power differs between exercises, so one percentage does not fit all.
rows: Power clean and hang power clean

entries.title: Ordinary lifts make poor power exercises because the bar has to be slowed
entries.take: A squat or bench press starts and ends at rest, so part of every fast rep is spent braking. Throws, jumps and Olympic lifts let you accelerate to the end.
entries.body: McDonald's explanation is mechanical. Training power means accelerating through the whole movement. In a normal lift the bar must stop at lockout, so the lifter eases off or the joints take the shock, and the lighter the load the longer the braking. Exercises in which the load or the body is released avoid this. A review of power training names ballistic, plyometric and weightlifting exercises as effective main exercises, and the 2026 ACSM stand found power was enhanced by Olympic-style lifting and fast lifting. His practical list is medicine-ball throws, kettlebell swings and jumps.
do: For power, choose exercises you can finish at full speed: throws, jumps, swings.
Avoid releasing a loaded bar without equipment built to catch it.

entries.title: Olympic lifts build power only once they can be done well with real loads
entries.take: The lifts are fast by nature and produce very high power, but they take a long time to learn. Short on time, use simpler explosive exercises.
entries.body: In a snatch or clean the bar is in effect thrown upward while the lifter drops under it, so nothing has to be braked. A meta-analysis found power cleans produced their highest power at 70% of max or more, well above the best load for a squat. McDonald's reservation is the learning time. With years to develop an athlete and a coach who can teach the lifts, he thinks they repay the effort. With four to eight weeks, or a large group, he would use jumps and throws that can be loaded after minutes of practice. Versions caught high, without the full squat, need less mobility but are still technical.
do: Learn the lifts from a qualified coach or leave them out.
Use jumps and throws for power while your lifting technique is still developing.

entries.title: Carrying on with jumps, throws or fast lifts after the snap has gone
entries.take: Power work only trains power while each rep is near your best. Slower reps add fatigue and nothing else.
entries.body: In growth and endurance training, fatigue is part of the stimulus. McDonald stresses that in power training it is not. Once bar speed, jump height or throw distance drops, the set has stopped doing its job, and when a new set opens with a flat rep the drill is over for the day. That keeps sets short and volume low, and it is why doing cleans or box jumps for high reps against the clock is conditioning, not power training. The 2026 ACSM stand found power was enhanced by low to moderate volumes with a fast lifting phase.
do: End a power set at the first clearly slower rep.
Keep jump, throw and fast-lift work early in the session, before fatiguing work.

entries.title: Longest useful all-out power set
entries.take: McDonald's limit for holding maximal power, after which output falls. He pairs sets this short with rests of 3 minutes or more.

entries.title: Use a mark, a tape or a stopwatch to judge power work
entries.take: A target to reach on every rep shows when a set should end and whether you are improving, with no electronics.
entries.body: Devices that read bar speed exist, but McDonald describes cheaper checks that coaches have long used. For a vertical jump, find the day's best height and set a mark there; the set ends when you miss it. For medicine-ball throws, measure distance and stop when it falls short. For bounds, count the distance covered in a fixed number of jumps. For sprints, time each run and stop once you are clearly off your best. A measurable target also motivates, and it shows over weeks whether power is rising. Without any measure, he says the lifter can usually feel the rep where the spring has gone.
do: Set a visible target for each power exercise.
Stop the exercise for the day when you miss the target on a first rep.

entries.title: For fast lifting on ordinary exercises, take 20 to 30% off your working weight
entries.take: A lifter who normally works at 80 to 85% of max lands at about 50 to 65% this way, inside the range where squats and bench presses produce most power.
entries.body: McDonald's quick rule avoids testing a max. Someone who benches 100 kg (220 lb) for sets of 5 would use 70 to 80 kg (155 to 175 lb), for sets of 3 to 5 reps and about 15 to 25 reps in all, with rests long enough to keep every rep fast. He stays toward the heavier end of the power range on ordinary lifts, because the lighter the bar, the more of each rep is spent braking it. Meta-analyses place peak power for the squat and bench press between 30 and 70% of max. He holds the load steady for weeks and raises it only when a small test increase leaves bar speed unchanged.
do: Take 20 to 30% off your usual working weight for fast sets.
Do 3 to 5 reps a set and stop when the bar slows.

entries.title: Reduction from working weight for fast, explosive sets
entries.take: McDonald's shortcut for lifters who train at about 80 to 85% of max. It gives roughly 50 to 65% of max, within the power range.

entries.title: Try to move a heavy bar fast even when it moves slowly
entries.take: In a 16-week trial, trying to move explosively produced the same high-speed adaptations whether or not the limb moved.
entries.body: Sixteen people trained one ankle with explosive efforts against a resistance that could not move, and the other with fast movements. After 16 weeks both sides showed the same gains at high speed, including a 26% rise in the rate of force development. The authors concluded that the repeated attempt to contract explosively was the main stimulus. McDonald applies this to heavy lifting: once technique is secure, drive every rep as fast as possible. He still expects heavy lifting combined with truly fast exercise such as jumps to beat either alone, because only real speed conditions the tissues for it.
do: On heavy sets with solid technique, push each rep up as fast as you can.
Lower the weight under control.

entries.title: Holding off all jumping until you can squat twice your body weight
entries.take: The old rule was written for depth jumps, the hardest plyometric drill. Easy hops, jumps and throws need no strength threshold.
entries.body: McDonald traces the rule to a time when plyometrics meant depth jumps, in which the athlete drops from a box and rebounds. Applied to all jumping, it would keep many athletes from any explosive work for two or three years. His approach is to bring in low-level work early and in small amounts: ankle hops, standing jumps, medicine-ball throws and kettlebell swings, often as part of the warm-up before lifting. That teaches the movements and lets tissue adapt while strength is built. Intense drills come later. The cautions are to teach landing, watch for shin and ankle trouble, and do less when unsure.
do: Add a few easy jumps or throws to your warm-up from early in training.
Save depth jumps and loaded jumps until you are strong and well practised.

entries.title: Order a session from fast and skilled work to slow and fatiguing work
entries.take: Speed, skill and power suffer most from fatigue, so they come first. Heavy strength follows, then higher-rep work, then conditioning.
entries.body: McDonald's rule is that whatever needs the highest quality goes first. In practice that gives four stages: skill and sprint work, then jumps, throws and fast lifts, then heavy strength work, then higher-rep muscle work and conditioning. Fast work done first costs later strength work little; heavy lifting done first ruins speed. Position stands agree. The 2009 ACSM stand puts multi-joint before single-joint and higher-intensity before lower-intensity exercises, and the 2026 stand found strength was enhanced when a lift was done early in the session. Few sessions hold more than two or three of these stages.
do: Put jumps, throws and Olympic lifts before heavy squats or presses.
Leave high-rep sets and conditioning for the end or another session.

entries.title: Post-activation potentiation and complex training
entries.take: A short rise in explosive performance after a few heavy efforts. Complex training alternates heavy sets with jumps to use it. A meta-analysis of 47 studies found small to moderate effects, larger in stronger, more experienced lifters.

entries.title: Power work is progressed slowly, by output more than by load
entries.take: Throwing further and jumping higher at the same load is the progress. Added weight changes these exercises more than it seems.
entries.body: In strength and growth training, load or reps go up as often as possible. McDonald describes power training differently. A 1 kg (2 lb) increase on a 4 kg (9 lb) medicine ball is 25%, enough to change the exercise, so ball weight is rarely raised. Jumps are loaded, if at all, with a vest starting at 2 to 3% of body weight and seldom above 10%. Progress comes from higher output on the same drill, an occasional extra set, and a slow move from easier drills to harder ones over months. He regards this work as general preparation: the thing an athlete is trying to overload is the sport, and power drills support it.
do: Record jump height or throw distance, and treat an increase at the same load as progress.

entries.title: After a true maximal personal best, end that work for the day
entries.take: A new best on an all-out lift or sprint is a stress the body has not met before. Stacking more on top can cost weeks.
entries.body: McDonald passes on a rule from an elite sprint-cycling coach and agrees with it. On truly maximal work, an athlete who misses the target on the first effort is too tired to improve that day and goes home. An athlete who sets a personal best also stops, because several bests in one session left riders flat for weeks afterwards. He links this to powerlifters who feel drained for a week after a meet of only nine heavy lifts, and limits the rule to maximal efforts. In submaximal training such as most growth work, a rep record takes far less out of you and needs no special handling.
do: After a new one-rep max, do no further maximal attempts that day.
If warm-ups show you are well off your usual numbers, cut the heavy work.

entries.title: Metabolic (depletion) training
entries.take: Weight training with light loads, sets of 15 to 20 or more and rests of a minute or less. It empties muscle glycogen and builds tolerance for fatigue more than it builds size or strength.

entries.title: High-rep, short-rest training builds fatigue tolerance more than size or strength
entries.take: Light loads, 15 to 20 reps and rests under a minute suit muscular endurance and work capacity. McDonald rates them a poor main method for growth.
entries.body: The 2009 ACSM stand describes local muscular endurance training as light to moderate loads of 40 to 60% of one-rep max for more than 15 reps, with rests under 90 seconds. McDonald's metabolic or depletion work is close: about 60% or less, 15 to 20 reps, 30 to 60 seconds of rest and three or four sets. He lists its uses as muscular endurance, a couple of weeks of work-capacity building, a rest for the joints from heavy loading and glycogen depletion in certain diets. Endurance rests on strength, so he would not use it alone. For growth he limits it to a few finishing sets after heavier work.
do: Use short blocks of high-rep work to build tolerance for training, then return to heavier loads.

entries.title: Switching to light weights and high reps to get lean
entries.take: High-rep circuits burn energy but hold muscle and strength poorly, and holding muscle is the main job of lifting during a diet.
entries.body: The habit of swapping heavy training for light, fast, high-rep work before a contest comes from bodybuilding. McDonald's argument is that it took hold in an era when anabolic steroids protected muscle whatever the training looked like, and that drug-free lifters who copy it give up the stimulus that tells the body to keep muscle. He grants that it uses more energy than heavy sets and empties muscle glycogen. His position is that it can be added in small amounts during a diet but must not replace heavier work, with complete beginners as the one exception. The diet area covers how heavy training protects lean mass.
do: Keep your usual heavy sets when you diet, with fewer sets if recovery drops.
Treat high-rep circuits as an optional extra, not the base of the plan.

entries.title: Building high-rep circuits around technical barbell lifts
entries.take: Under heavy fatigue, squat technique changes within the session. Simple exercises are the safer choice for high-rep, short-rest work.
entries.body: Twenty-five people with at least six months of barbell experience did a highly fatiguing workout that included 55 squat repetitions. Knee and hip angles shifted, with less knee bend and more forward lean, and the authors concluded that such changes may raise injury risk. McDonald makes the same point from coaching: squats or deadlifts for sets of 15 to 20 on short rests invite a loss of form even when the load is light, and high-rep Olympic lifts are worse for anyone without years of practice. He builds these sessions from machines and other low-skill exercises.
do: Use machines, simple dumbbell moves or easy bodyweight exercises for circuits.
Keep squats, deadlifts and Olympic lifts for sets where you are fresh.

entries.title: Hypertrophy and hyperplasia
entries.take: Hypertrophy is the enlargement of existing muscle fibres. Hyperplasia would be a rise in the number of fibres. Growth from training in humans is explained by hypertrophy; hyperplasia is unproven and, in McDonald's view, minor at most.

entries.title: Myofibrillar and sarcoplasmic hypertrophy
entries.take: Myofibrillar growth adds contractile protein, the part of a fibre that produces force. Sarcoplasmic growth is a disproportionate expansion of the fluid and stored material around it.

entries.title: Every training style builds both contractile protein and muscle volume
entries.take: Some evidence shows the fluid part of a fibre can expand faster than its contractile protein, but no method produces one kind of growth alone.
entries.body: A 2020 review found select evidence that sarcoplasmic hypertrophy coincides with fibre growth during resistance training, alongside evidence for growth in which contractile protein keeps pace or even leads. The idea is used to explain why some large lifters are not proportionally strong. McDonald thinks the distinction has some merit, and his impression is that lifters who train only for the pump lose size faster when they stop. He is clear that the difference is one of emphasis: bodybuilders who train with high reps build real contractile tissue, and heavy lifters gain muscle volume too.
do: Choose rep ranges for your goal and your joints, not to target one kind of growth.

entries.title: Mechanical tension is the main growth signal; damage and burn are secondary
entries.take: Reviews rank mechanical signals as the prime trigger for hypertrophy. Muscle damage is probably not needed, and metabolic stress looks minor.
entries.body: A 2019 review of hypertrophy stimuli names mechanical signals as the prime candidates and says exercise-induced damage is probably not essential. A separate review concluded that damage neither mediates nor potentiates growth. McDonald puts tension first and now largely discounts damage. He reads the growth seen with very light loads taken to failure as tension reached the slow way. His practical test is strength in moderate rep ranges over the years. A lifter benching the same weight for the same reps a year later has probably not grown, and one lifting clearly more for those reps probably has.
do: Track a few lifts in a moderate rep range and aim to raise them over months.
Do not use soreness or the pump as the measure of a productive session.

entries.title: The hormone rise after a session does not decide how much you grow
entries.take: In 49 trained men, the post-exercise rise in hormones was unrelated to gains in muscle or strength over 12 weeks.
entries.body: Short rests and big lifts are often promoted for the hormone rise they cause. Forty-nine resistance-trained men did 12 weeks of whole-body training with either light loads for 20 to 25 reps or heavier loads for 8 to 12, all sets to failure. Muscle fibre size and lean mass rose equally, and no significant correlation appeared between the acute rise in any measured hormone and the change in strength or size. McDonald's reading of the wider literature is the same: these brief shifts are at most a tiny part of the growth stimulus.
do: Choose rest times that let you repeat your reps, not ones meant to raise hormones.

entries.title: McDonald's growth guideline for reps in a session
entries.take: His working range at about 60 to 85% of max, citing a 2007 review he reads as favouring 30 to 60. Newer analyses count weekly sets.

entries.title: Muscles already worked by compound lifts need about half the direct work
entries.take: After pressing or rowing, the arms and rear shoulders have done part of their work. McDonald halves their direct volume.
entries.body: A bench press trains the chest, the front of the shoulders and the triceps, and a row trains the back and the biceps. McDonald's rule of thumb, which he presents as experience and says he has not seen tested, is that a smaller muscle trained after the compound work for a larger one needs about half the usual direct volume: roughly 20 to 30 reps, or two to four sets. He applies it to triceps after chest, biceps after back and rear shoulders after rows. In his view the front of the shoulder rarely needs direct work in a plan with pressing, while the side of the shoulder gains from a raise as well as a press.
do: Count pressing and rowing sets as partial work for the arms and shoulders.
Give the arms about half the direct sets you give the chest or back that day.

entries.title: Match the exercise to the rep range
entries.take: Heavy sets of 5 to 8 suit compound lifts. Sets of 12 to 20 suit exercises with no weak link and little danger if form slips.
entries.body: McDonald's guide is practical. In low rep ranges, big compound lifts such as squats, presses, rows and leg presses handle the load well, while single-joint exercises done that heavy put a lot of stress on one joint. In high rep ranges the problem reverses. Long sets of a compound lift tend to end when a smaller muscle tires, such as the lower back in a squat or the arms in a press or row, and form can slip while the bar is still loaded. For those sets he prefers machines and single-joint exercises that keep the work on the target muscle. Between about 6 and 12 reps either kind works, and build and skill decide.
do: Do your heaviest, lowest-rep work on compound lifts.
Move high-rep sets to machines or single-joint exercises if a small muscle gives out first.

entries.title: Doing three or four near-identical exercises for one muscle
entries.take: Barbell, dumbbell and machine versions of the same press train a muscle the same way. The extra exercises only add sets.
entries.body: McDonald traces the habit to high-volume bodybuilding of the steroid era, and thinks it leads drug-free lifters to do too many sets. His guideline is one or two exercises for a muscle in a session. The back is the exception at three or four, because it is several muscles with different jobs. Where a second exercise is used he wants it to differ in kind: a heavy compound lift, then one that loads the muscle at long length or one that is hardest in the shortened position. He keeps the same exercises through a block of six to eight weeks so progress can be tracked, and swaps them between blocks.
do: Limit most muscles to one or two exercises in a session.
Make a second exercise different in kind, not the same movement on other equipment.

entries.title: Growth programmes that last share the same few ingredients
entries.take: Plans that look very different on paper all combine progressive loading, some fatigue work, moderate volume and regular easier weeks.
entries.body: McDonald compares several well-known hypertrophy systems, among them Bryan Haycock's HST, Dante Trudell's DC training, Borge Fagerli's Myo-reps and his own generic bulking routine. He finds the same core in each: weight on the bar is pushed up over time, there is some higher-rep or short-rest work, volume for a muscle is moderate, each muscle is trained more than once a week, and hard weeks alternate with easier ones. His conclusion is that a plan lacking those ingredients is the one to doubt. The 2026 ACSM overview likewise found few prescription details changed outcomes.
do: Check a new programme for progression, sensible volume and planned easier weeks before its details.

entries.title: Treating 8 to 12 reps as the only range that builds muscle
entries.take: Growth has been shown across a wide span of loads. The 8 to 12 range is a convenient middle, not a boundary.
entries.body: A network meta-analysis of 28 studies in 747 adults found muscle growth was independent of load when sets were taken to failure, while strength gains were larger with heavier loads. McDonald wrote years earlier that he could find no original research behind 8 to 12 as the growth range, and placed growth training anywhere from about 5 to 20 reps. He notes that Olympic weightlifters add size with sets of five. His practical limits are at the edges: very low reps need many sets and are hard on joints, and very high reps are painful and inefficient.
do: Use any rep range from about 5 to 20 that lets you train the muscle hard.
Choose the range by the exercise and by what your joints tolerate.

entries.title: Repetition continuum
entries.take: The idea that low, moderate and high reps lean toward strength, size and endurance in turn. The zones overlap: the heavy end of size training is the light end of strength training.

entries.title: Volume load (tonnage)
entries.take: Sets multiplied by reps multiplied by the weight lifted, added up over a session or a week. Three sets of 5 with 100 kg (220 lb) is 1,500 kg (3,300 lb).

entries.title: Three ways to count training volume
entries.take: Each count answers a different question and each can mislead. The comparison follows Lyle McDonald's discussion of volume.
rows: Sets taken close to failure, for each muscle each week
Planning growth training; the unit in recent dose-response analyses
Treats a set of 3 and a set of 12 as equal
Reps for a muscle in a session, at about 60 to 85% of max
Comparing schemes that use different reps per set
Ignores how hard each set was
Tracking workload on the same lift over time
Inflated by short-range heavy lifts and by large amounts of light work

entries.title: Technical failure
entries.take: The point in a set where good form can no longer be kept, even if a rougher rep is still possible. On skilled lifts it comes before momentary muscular failure and is the safer place to stop.

entries.title: Use an occasional all-out last set to check your working weight
entries.take: Every three or four weeks, push the last set as far as it will go. Far more reps than the target means the weight is too light.
entries.body: People tend to underestimate how many reps they have left. A review of 12 studies found an average underprediction of about one rep, with wide variation, and McDonald reports newer lifters stopping at 10 when 5 or 6 more were possible. His check is simple. If the plan is four sets of 8, do three as written and take the fourth as far as good form allows. Getting 9 or 10 means the load is right. Getting 12 or more means it should go up. He uses the test every three or four weeks, not on every exercise, because sets to failure cost recovery and, for some lifters, spoil the sets that follow.
do: Every few weeks, take the last set of a main exercise to failure with good form.
Raise the weight if you beat the target by four or more reps.

entries.title: Four kinds of weight training and the loading that defines each
entries.take: Loads, reps and rests from the 2009 and 2026 ACSM position stands. The zones overlap, and most programmes use more than one.
rows: The most weight you can lift once
80% of 1RM or more (2026); 1 to 6RM emphasised for trained lifters (2009)
30 to 70% of 1RM, lifted as fast as possible (2026)
Low to moderate volume (2026); 3 to 5 sets (2009)
A wide range works; 6 to 12RM emphasised in 2009
Higher volume: at least 10 weekly sets enhanced growth (2026)
1 to 2 minutes (2009); the hypertrophy area has newer rest findings

entries.title: Load intensity and effort intensity
entries.take: Two different meanings of intensity. Intensity of load is the weight as a share of your one-rep max. Intensity of effort is how close the set comes to failure, often given as RPE or reps in reserve.

entries.title: Repetition maximum (RM) load
entries.take: The top weight a lifter can manage for a stated number of reps in good form. A 10RM is a load you can lift ten times and not eleven. A zone such as 8 to 12RM sets the load without a percentage.

entries.title: Describe a set with two numbers: how heavy and how hard
entries.take: The same weight can be an easy set or an all-out one. Load says how heavy the bar is; effort says how near failure the set went.
entries.body: McDonald's point is that most arguments about intensity come from people using one word for two things. Two reps at 85% of max and five reps at 85% share a load intensity but are very different efforts. Twelve reps to failure at about 75% is a moderate load and a maximal effort. Fast sets at 30 to 60% are light, yet each rep is pushed as hard as possible. He suggests recording both, an approach he credits to the powerlifting coach Mike Tuchscherer, and adds looser senses of the word: low reps are demanding on the nervous system, moderate reps on the muscle, and very high reps on energy supply.
do: Log the weight and reps, then add how many reps you had left.

entries.title: Outside the lifting sports, set loads by a rep-max zone, not a percentage
entries.take: A percentage needs a tested max and assumes everyone gets the same reps at it. A rep zone with a few reps in reserve needs neither.
entries.body: McDonald lists the problems of percent-based loading for non-specialists: testing a true max takes skill and carries risk, the max shifts from week to week, and the reps possible at a given percentage differ between people. A meta-regression of 269 studies supports the last point, with a spread of about 2.5 reps around the average at 80% of max. His method is to choose a zone such as 10 to 15RM. Fewer than 10 reps means the weight is too heavy, and more than 15 means it is too light. Sets stop a few reps short of failure, and the weight goes up once the last set leaves two or three in hand.
do: Pick a rep zone for each exercise and find the weight that fits it.
Raise the weight when your last set ends with two or three reps to spare.

entries.title: All-out fast work needs a longer warm-up than its light loads suggest
entries.take: A sprint, jump or throw is a maximal effort even with no load, so the warm-up should build to full speed in steps.
entries.body: The usual rule is that harder work needs more warm-up: an easy jog needs none, and heavy singles need many build-up sets. McDonald points out that power and speed work break the pattern people expect. The load is light but nothing is held back, and going straight to full speed is how shoulders and hamstrings get hurt. Sprinters commonly spend 30 to 45 minutes on easy running, mobility work, drills and build-up runs before the first full sprint. In the gym, he suggests a few progressively faster or heavier sets of the movement itself, and notes that power work done after sprint or skill practice needs less.
do: Before maximal jumps, throws or sprints, do several build-up efforts at rising speed.
Never make the first rep of the day an all-out one.

entries.title: General and specific warm-up
entries.take: A general warm-up is light whole-body activity that raises body temperature. A specific warm-up is progressively heavier sets of the exercise you are about to train, which also rehearse technique and ready the nervous system.

entries.title: End the general warm-up at a light sweat
entries.take: Five to ten minutes of easy activity is typical. The endpoint is feeling warm, and many lifters can use light first sets instead.
entries.body: McDonald prefers a sign to a stopwatch: continue until sweating lightly, which takes longer in a cold room and for older or very fit people. Any easy whole-body activity works. He treats it as optional for young, uninjured lifters, who can start with light sets of the first exercise. Evidence gives it some support. Thirteen trained people leg-pressed 8.4% more on a one-rep-max test after 20 minutes of easy cycling plus warm-up sets than after the warm-up sets alone, and a meta-analysis found warm-ups improved performance in 79% of the measures examined.
do: Do a few minutes of easy movement until you feel warm, then start your ramp-up sets.
Take longer in the cold, or if your joints are stiff.

entries.title: How many warm-up sets, by situation
entries.take: Lyle McDonald's guidance gathered into one comparison. Heavier loads, more technical lifts and stronger lifters need more sets.
