entries.title: Warm-up sets before heavy triples
entries.take: McDonald's guide for work at about 85 to 90% of max. Sets of 12 at moderate loads need only one or two.

entries.title: Taking warm-up sets close to failure
entries.take: High-rep sets on the way up tire you before the sets that count. Keep warm-up sets short and cut the reps as the weight rises.
entries.body: The old ascending pyramid starts with 12 to 15 hard reps and adds weight each set, so the lifter reaches the heaviest set already tired. McDonald prefers a ramp of short sets: roughly four steps from about half the working weight to just under it, with reps falling from five or more to singles, 30 to 60 seconds between steps and about two minutes before the first work set. Exact percentages do not matter; sensible plate jumps do. A squat trial fits this: adding heavier or faster warm-up sets did not increase the reps lifters could do afterwards compared with their usual warm-up.
do: Do fewer reps on each warm-up set as the bar gets heavier.
Finish every warm-up set well short of fatigue.

entries.title: End a warm-up set at the rep where the weight starts to feel easy
entries.take: Reps in a warm-up set often feel stiff, then suddenly smooth. That change is a better stopping point than a fixed count.
entries.body: McDonald passes on a cue from his own mentor. During a warm-up set the first reps tend to feel heavy and awkward, and at some point, perhaps the fourth rep or the eighth, one moves freely. He ends the set there and adds weight for the next one. The number differs between people and between days, which is why he treats published rep counts as a guide. He also wants warm-up reps done with full attention, since they are extra practice of the lift, and notes that experienced athletes put the same care into them as into their work sets. Beginners gain most from this, provided the reps are deliberate.
do: Stop each warm-up set when a rep first feels smooth, then go up.
Treat every warm-up rep as technique practice.

entries.title: Stretch before lifting where tightness blocks a safe position
entries.take: Static holds up to 30 to 45 seconds did not reduce maximal muscle performance in a review of 106 studies. Longer holds did, when tested straight afterwards.
entries.body: A systematic review found no harm from static stretches under 30 seconds, none of significance at 30 to 45 seconds, and likely reductions at 60 seconds or more. McDonald adds that such studies test performance right after stretching, while a lifter goes on to ramp-up sets. His rule is practical. If tight hips make the lower back round in a squat, or tight shoulders spoil the bench press set-up, stretch them first, since position matters more than a percent or two of force. Otherwise he uses dynamic movement or progressively deeper light sets before training, and keeps long static holds for afterwards.
do: Before lifting, stretch only the areas that stop you reaching a good position.
Keep any pre-lift static hold under about 30 seconds.

entries.title: Static, dynamic and ballistic stretching
entries.take: Static stretching holds a muscle at length without moving. Dynamic stretching moves a joint under control through a range that grows with each rep. Ballistic stretching flings the limb through the range and has fallen out of favour.

entries.title: Foam rolling before lifting is optional and does not replace warming up
entries.take: Rolling before exercise gave a small gain in flexibility and a negligible change in strength in a meta-analysis of 21 studies.
entries.body: A meta-analysis of 21 studies, 14 of them on rolling before exercise, found it improved flexibility by about 4% and sprint performance by 0.7%, with negligible effects on jumping and strength. McDonald places it as an extra for people with long-standing tight or troublesome tissue, done before any stretching, and points out that it does little to raise tissue temperature. He takes the same line on activation drills such as glute bridges or band walks: useful for a muscle that is plainly not doing its share, and a poor use of half a session for everyone else.
do: Roll or do activation drills only for a specific, known problem.
Keep the whole warm-up short enough that it never eats into the session.

entries.title: A single at the working weight is an optional primer for experienced lifters
entries.take: Some lifters find the first work set easier after one rep at that weight. Trial evidence for a benefit is thin.
entries.body: McDonald offers this only to lifters with a settled basic warm-up. If your second work set usually feels better than your first, one rep at the working weight before the first set may help. With higher-rep work he sometimes uses a single slightly above the working weight, or a 6 to 10 second hold of a load about 10% heavier, to make the work sets feel light. He avoids it when the work itself is sets of three or fewer, where it only adds fatigue. The research is mixed: potentiation effects on explosive tasks are small and larger in stronger people, and a squat trial found no gain in reps from heavier warm-up sets.
do: Try a single at the working weight if your first set is always your worst.
Drop it if it makes no difference after a few sessions.

entries.title: Five sets of five (5x5)
entries.take: A strength routine of five sets of five reps on a few compound lifts, popularised by Bill Starr in a book for football players and revived by later barbell programmes. The label covers several quite different set plans.

entries.title: Ramped sets and sets across
entries.take: Ramped sets rise in weight from set to set, so only the last one or two are hard. Sets across use the same working weight for every set, after separate warm-up sets.

entries.title: Five rising sets of five suit learning a lift, if someone checks the technique
entries.take: Each session gives 25 practice reps that end in one challenging set. Without a coach, lifters tend to add weight faster than their form allows.
entries.body: In the beginner version the five sets climb to a single hard set, and the starting weights move up a little each session. McDonald rates it highly for teaching a lift or returning to one after a layoff. The early sets are light enough to do perfectly, each heavier set asks for more tightness and concentration, and three sessions a week add up to nearly a thousand practice reps over twelve weeks. If technique slips he holds the weight for the remaining sets. His warning is that an unsupervised lifter will usually load the bar too quickly, and for that person he considers a higher rep range the safer way to start.
do: Use the ramp while learning a lift, with a coach or video to check each session.
Stay at the same weight for the rest of the sets when form slips.

entries.title: For five sets of five at one weight, use about 75 to 80% of max
entries.take: A true five-rep max cannot be repeated for five sets. The working weight has to sit below it, and total reps show whether it is right.
entries.body: A single all-out set of five is roughly 85% of a one-rep max. McDonald puts five sets at one weight at about 75 to 80%, after warm-up sets, for only a few lifts in a session. He passes on two checks used with this plan: fewer than 14 reps out of the 25 means the weight is too heavy, and a sharp drop after the first couple of sets is a sign to stop for the day. When all 25 reps are made, add 2.5 to 5 kg (5 to 10 lb) on the squat, bench press or deadlift and about half that elsewhere. The loading matches an older meta-analysis in which trained people gained most strength at a mean of 80% and four sets.
do: Start five-by-five at a weight you could lift 8 times.
Add weight only after completing all 25 reps.

entries.title: Load that allows five sets of five at one weight
entries.take: McDonald's working range for 5x5 with the same weight. A single maximal set of five is about 85%.

entries.title: What five sets of five does well, and where it falls short
entries.take: It is a sound way to build base strength and some size. It is not a peaking plan, and it leans on lifts that need coaching.
entries.body: McDonald's verdict is favourable with limits. Sets of five are heavy enough to build strength, the 2026 ACSM stand found loads of 80% or more enhanced it, and five sets supply useful volume while fatigue stays low enough for technique to hold. His reservations: powerlifters need more heavy singles, doubles and triples than it provides, and plans built on three barbell lifts are hard to learn alone and leave gaps he would fill with rows, pulldowns and arm work. For a lifter who stalls, he suggests dropping one set at a time while still adding weight, then cutting the load 15 to 20% and starting again.
do: Use 5x5 for one or two main lifts and train the rest with higher reps.
When progress stalls, cut sets before you cut the weight.

entries.title: 20-rep squat (breathing squat)
entries.take: An old rest-pause method: one set of 20 squats with a weight you could normally lift about 10 times, made possible by standing with the bar and taking several deep breaths between reps.

entries.title: The 20-rep squat teaches effort, but its famous weight-gain claims do not hold up
entries.take: One all-out set shows a lifter how far real limits lie beyond perceived ones. Rapid weight gained on such a plan is not mostly muscle.
entries.body: McDonald describes the set as roughly 10 continuous reps followed by 10 near-maximal singles, each after as many breaths as needed, with the bar on the back for several minutes. He thinks most lifters would learn from one short cycle, because finishing the set proves they had been stopping early. He rejects two traditional claims: gains on the scale of 30 lb (14 kg) in six weeks cannot be mostly muscle, and the light pullovers once paired with the squat do not expand the rib cage. He ran it for months himself and came to dread sessions, so he now advises short cycles only.
do: Treat it as an occasional short block, not a year-round programme.

entries.title: Break in below your 10-rep max and keep a 20-rep squat cycle short
entries.take: Start 10 to 20% under your best 10-rep weight, add a little each time you make 20, and stop after four to eight weeks.
entries.body: McDonald's first rule is never to open with a true 10-rep max: use 10 to 20% less for the first two or three weeks so the back and breathing can adapt. Add about 2.5 kg (5 lb) whenever all 20 reps are made. Do the set once a week with a lighter leg day, or every fifth day; twice a week is the most he thinks anyone recovers from. Keep the whole cycle to four to six weeks, eight at most, then take several easy days. A set this long under a heavy bar should be done in a rack with safety bars, and is not for anyone with back, heart or blood pressure problems unless a clinician agrees.
do: Squat inside a rack with the safety bars set just below your bottom position.
End the set if your back position goes, whatever the rep count.

entries.title: Applying the 20-rep grind to deadlifts or good mornings
entries.take: Technique in these lifts breaks down quickly as reps climb, and the part that fails is the back.
entries.body: Versions of the breathing-squat idea have been published for the deadlift and the good morning. McDonald advises against both. A squat that goes wrong late in a long set can usually be set down on the safety bars. A deadlift or good morning taken to that level of fatigue tends to finish with a rounded back under load, and he notes that one magazine author who recommended the 20-rep deadlift was injured for months by it. He tried it once and did not repeat it. Rest-pause methods on machines or upper-body lifts are a different matter, since a failed rep there carries little risk.
do: Keep very long, all-out sets to exercises where a failed rep is safe.

entries.title: Weider principles
entries.take: Names such as the superset, split routine and drop set principles, attached by the publisher Joe Weider to methods lifters already used. They are labels from his magazines, not discoveries; the hypertrophy area covers what the methods do.

entries.title: The 300, 400, 500 rule is a long-term target for an average-sized man
entries.take: A strict bench press of 300 lb (136 kg), squat of 400 lb (181 kg) and deadlift of 500 lb (227 kg) is an old estimate of where a drug-free lifter nears his muscular limit.
entries.body: The rule was popularised by Stuart McRobert, and Lyle McDonald sets out the conditions people leave off. It assumes a man of about 86 to 91 kg (190 to 200 lb) and average height, so smaller lifters should expect less and bigger ones more. It assumes strict lifts: a controlled bench press with no bounce or help, a squat below parallel, a deadlift without hitching. It assumes equal work on all three, and ideally the weights are handled for several reps. McDonald says it does not translate to women. It is a rule of thumb from coaching, not a population norm, and many lifters never reach it.
do: Use the figures as distant goals, scaled to your body weight.

entries.title: The 300, 400, 500 rule as multiples of body weight
entries.take: Bench press, squat and deadlift for a man of about 90 kg (200 lb), as McDonald works out McRobert's rule. A coaching target, not a norm.

entries.title: Top-tenth relative strength in drug-tested, unequipped powerlifters
entries.take: 90th-percentile lifts for competitors aged 18 to 35, from 809,986 competition entries, beside the McRobert target for an average man.

entries.title: In unequipped lifting the deadlift is biggest, then the squat, then the bench press
entries.take: Norms from over 800,000 drug-tested, unequipped competition entries show that order at the 90th percentile for both sexes.
entries.body: Among competitors aged 18 to 35, the 90th-percentile man deadlifted 3.25 times body weight, squatted 2.83 and benched 1.95; for women the figures were 2.66, 2.26 and 1.35. McDonald explains why a squat larger than a deadlift is mostly an artefact. Supportive suits add far more to the squat, some federations pass squats that are cut high, and a legal squat has to pass through a deep sticking point that the deadlift's higher start avoids. Build still shifts the gap: one of his lifters deadlifts over 45 kg (100 lb) more than she squats. A gym squat well above your deadlift is a reason to check your depth.
do: If your squat exceeds your deadlift, film it from the side and check depth.

entries.title: Comparing your lifts with numbers that carry no conditions
entries.take: A lift only compares with a standard done the same way: same depth, no bounce or help, same body weight and sex, and no drugs or supportive suits.
entries.body: McDonald's test is to ask how many strict lifts at the 300, 400 and 500 lb (136, 181 and 227 kg) level you have seen from a lifter of about 90 kg (200 lb) in an ordinary gym. His guess is between none and two, because most big numbers quoted in gyms come from half squats, bounced or assisted bench presses, or much heavier people. Records mislead in the other direction: they describe the rare outlier, as the top tenth of drug-tested competitors shows with squats near 2.8 times body weight for men. A fair comparison needs the lift's conditions and the lifter's body weight attached.
do: Record your own lifts to a fixed standard of depth and control.
Compare yourself with lifters of your sex, size and training history.

entries.title: The stronger you are, the slower strength comes
entries.take: Across 15 years of competition results, the strongest quarter of men gained strength at about half the daily rate of the least strong quarter.
entries.body: Researchers tracked 1,897 powerlifters between 2003 and 2018. Men in the strongest quarter at their first meet gained strength at 0.102 kg (0.22 lb) a day, against 0.211 kg (0.47 lb) for the least strong quarter, which the authors attribute to a possible ceiling effect. Women's rates did not differ by starting strength. This fits McDonald's framing of targets such as 300, 400 and 500 as goals for years of work, reached by some lifters and not others. A plan that expects the monthly progress of a first-year lifter from a fifth-year lifter will always look as if it is failing.
do: Judge progress against your own recent rate, not your first-year rate.

entries.title: Outcome, performance and process goals
entries.take: An outcome goal is a result against others, such as winning. A performance goal is a standard of your own, such as a 100 kg (220 lb) squat. A process goal is an action you carry out, such as hitting depth on every rep.

entries.title: Goals about what you do beat goals about what you get
entries.take: In a meta-analysis of goal setting in sport, process goals improved performance far more than performance or outcome goals.
entries.body: Twenty-seven studies were pooled. Process goals had the largest effect on performance (d = 1.36), against 0.44 for performance goals and 0.09 for outcome goals. McDonald describes the same split in athletes. Those who live by results tend to be driven in the short term and burn out, because nobody wins or sets a record every time and each bad day feeds tension into the next. Those who judge a session by how well they carried it out still care about results, but they can take something from a bad day: the weak point it exposed. He prefers to coach the second kind.
do: Give each session one thing to do well, such as every squat to depth.
Review a bad session for the weak point it showed.

entries.title: Judging every session by whether you set a personal best
entries.take: Records cannot come every time. Treating each ordinary session as a failure builds tension that makes the next one worse.
entries.body: McDonald's picture of the outcome-driven lifter is someone who must lift more than last time whenever they train, and who reads one flat day as proof of weakness. The usual response is to try harder, which tightens technique, spoils the following session and starts a run of bad days. He adds, as his own impression from coaching, that men fall into this more often than women and are less willing to take weight off the bar to fix a lift. His remedy is to change what counts as success: aim to do the movement right and let the load follow. After a poor session he often backs off a little or shifts the focus.
do: Count a session as successful if the planned work was done with good form.
Respond to a bad day by easing off, not by forcing a heavier one.

entries.title: What a lifter can and cannot control
entries.take: Lyle McDonald's rule: accept the fixed factors, use them only to shape your approach, and put the effort into the rest.
columns: What you can do about it
rows: Which lifts suit you and how much you lift
Adjust grip, stance and style; strengthen the weak part of the lift
Fibre type and how well you respond to training
Rate of gain and the eventual ceiling
Train consistently and judge progress against your own past
Recovery and the speed of muscle gain
Sleep, eat enough, and match the workload to what you recover from
How appetite and metabolism react to dieting
Choose the diet structure you can keep to, and manage activity and sleep
Set process goals and compete against your own numbers

entries.title: Two questions can stand in for a coach
entries.take: Ask what you would tell another lifter in your position. And if you are wondering whether to do one more set, take that as a no.
entries.body: McDonald argues that self-coached lifters lack distance, so they talk themselves into what they want to do. His first check is to picture someone else in the same situation and follow the advice he would give them, unless there is a concrete reason his case differs. The second comes from his skating coach: doubt about another set or interval is itself the answer. By then the training effect is banked, and the extra one is where injuries happen. The second rule suits driven trainees, not people who look for reasons to stop. He once ignored it on a deadlift and lost nine months to a back strain.
do: Before changing the plan mid-session, ask what you would tell a friend to do.
When in doubt about one more set, stop.

entries.title: Adding sets, sessions and exercises to your own plan as you go
entries.take: Self-coached lifters rarely fail through laziness. They do too much, too often, and explain to themselves why they are the exception.
entries.body: McDonald reports that experienced coaches say the same of themselves: they would never let an athlete do what they do in their own training, adding sets and exercises until the volume has doubled. His skating coach's blunt fix was to write the programme and then cut it in half. Outside accountability helps too: he had friends ask whether he was sticking to his plan. Supervision has a measurable effect. A meta-analysis of 12 studies found supervised training produced moderately larger strength gains than unsupervised training (standardised effect 0.40) and little difference in body composition.
do: Write the plan before the session and do not add to it on the day.
Ask someone to check now and then that you are following it.

entries.title: A coach adds technique, restraint and a plan
entries.take: Supervised lifters gained more strength than unsupervised ones in pooled trials. The benefit is partly being pushed and partly being held back.
entries.body: McDonald lists three things a coach supplies. The first is technical feedback, which he thinks most gym-goers badly need. The second is effort in the right amount: reviews show people left alone choose loads averaging 53% of max, while driven athletes need the opposite, so he asks them whether they should do another set, never whether they want to. The third is control of the process, meaning how much, how hard and when to rest. Pooled trials back the general point, with a moderate strength advantage for supervised training across 12 studies. A coach must be able to teach good technique, which is not a given.
do: If you cannot hire a coach, film your lifts and have an experienced lifter review them.

entries.title: A simple plan carried out fully beats an elaborate one
entries.take: Coaches tend to overcomplicate in mid-career and simplify with experience. Evidence agrees that most programme details change little.
entries.body: McDonald describes three stages in a coach's development: knowing nothing, believing you know a great deal, and learning how much you do not know. The middle stage produces intricate periodisation charts that he found no more productive than hard work on basics. The 2026 ACSM overview of 137 reviews gives the same picture from data: few prescription variables affected the main adaptations, and set structure, time under tension, periodisation and training to failure did not consistently change outcomes. What remains is load heavy enough for the goal, enough weekly sets, progression and showing up.
do: Choose the simplest plan that covers load, weekly sets and progression.
Change one thing at a time, and only when progress has stopped.

entries.title: Sports select body types more than they build them
entries.take: There is no single athletic physique. Elite athletes look alike within a sport because those with the right build rise to the top.
entries.body: The slogan that athletic training gives an athletic look assumes the training creates the body. A review of athlete size over the twentieth century describes elite sport as selection: in many sports athletes grew taller and heavier faster than the population, while sports needing a narrow build kept the same sizes. McDonald's point: a sumo wrestler, a gymnast and a distance runner are all athletes, and copying their training will not give you their frames. When weightlifters need more muscle they add bodybuilding-style work after their lifting. For looks, train for muscle and manage body fat directly.
do: If appearance is the goal, use growth training and diet, not a sport's programme.

entries.title: Picking one habit of champions as the reason for their success
entries.take: The lifters who got nowhere usually had the same habit. What top performers share is a decade or more of consistent work, plus talent.
entries.body: McDonald's objection to the phrase about success leaving clues is that people choose the clue that suits what they are selling. Champion bodybuilders take supplements and train each muscle once a week; so do the far larger number who never succeed, and the champions mostly trained differently on the way up. A habit only counts as evidence if it separates those who succeeded from those who did not. His own list of what the best have in common is short: ten or more years of hard, sensible, consistent training toward one goal, and the talent that elite sport selects for. The rest he calls details.
do: Ask whether unsuccessful lifters do the same thing before you copy it.
Put consistency over years ahead of any single method.

entries.title: Lifting the weight fast adds a little to physical function in older adults
entries.take: In adults over 60, training with a fast lifting phase improved physical function modestly more than conventional strength training.
entries.body: A meta-analysis of 20 trials in 566 community-living adults aged 60 and over compared lifting as fast as possible with ordinary strength training. Power training was associated with a modest extra improvement in physical function (standardised difference 0.30), on low-certainty evidence. The 2026 ACSM stand also found power training enhanced physical function. McDonald notes that lost muscle power is part of declining function with age. His caution is about method: jumps and Olympic lifts carry too much risk for an unconditioned older person, so fast work belongs on simple, stable exercises.
do: Older lifters can push the lifting phase fast on machines or other stable exercises.
Get a clinician's clearance first if you have joint, heart or balance problems.

entries.title: For general health, two or three short full-body sessions cover the lifting
entries.take: Guidelines ask for resistance exercise for each major muscle group on two or three days a week. One to three sets of one or two exercises per muscle is enough.
entries.body: The ACSM's 2011 position stand recommends resistance exercise for each major muscle group on 2 to 3 days a week, and the World Health Organization recommends regular muscle-strengthening activity at every age. McDonald's reading is that health needs far less than size or performance: one to three sets, one or two exercises for each muscle, mostly moderate reps, and more sets when reps are lower. Any exercises that can be done safely will do, and getting the sessions done matters more than their details. Thirty minutes of lifting and thirty of cardio, three times a week, go a long way.
do: Lift two or three days a week, covering every major muscle group.
Keep sessions short enough that you never skip them.

entries.title: Occasional heavier sets and loaded standing lifts are worth including for bone
entries.take: Bone responds to heavy loading through the skeleton. A health-focused lifter gains from some sets of 5 or 6 without living there.
entries.body: In 101 postmenopausal women with low bone mass, eight months of supervised heavy lifting and impact work, built on five sets of five at over 85% of max, raised lumbar spine bone density by 2.9% while it fell 1.2% in a low-intensity home programme. McDonald advises people training for health to visit lower rep ranges from time to time for this reason, and to include lifts that load the spine and legs, such as squats or overhead presses. His caution is that constant heavy work wears on joints in older lifters, and that these lifts need competent teaching. Anyone with diagnosed low bone mass should be supervised.
do: Include a few weeks of sets of 5 or 6 on a well-learned lift in each training block.
With low bone density, start heavy loading only under professional supervision.

entries.title: Weekly layouts for all-round fitness
entries.take: Ways Lyle McDonald arranges lifting and cardio for general fitness, by the days available. All meet the guideline of lifting on two or three days.

About 30 minutes of each; sessions run long but nothing is missed
Lifting days spaced through the week
Lift on 3 alternate days, cardio on the 3 between
Equal emphasis on strength and aerobic fitness
3 to 4 lifting days plus 3 short cardio sessions
Run for 6 to 8 weeks, then switch emphasis
3 to 4 cardio sessions plus 2 brief lifting days
The lifting is enough to maintain strength

entries.title: After the first year, vary reps in simple ways
entries.take: Three easy options: step the reps down over weeks, progress inside one wide rep range, or use two rep ranges in the same week.
entries.body: McDonald suggests more structure only after 6 to 12 months of steady basic training. One option is to start at sets of 12 and move to 10, 8 and then 6 every two or three weeks, adding weight at each step, then take an easy week or two and begin again. A second is double progression in a range of 6 to 12. A third is one session in a higher range such as 10 to 12 and another in a lower one such as 6 to 8. He does not rank them: the best choice is the one a person will keep doing. A meta-analysis of 18 studies found periodised training produced larger one-rep-max gains than unvaried training.
do: Pick one scheme and run it for several months.
Take an easy week when a cycle of heavier weeks ends.

acsm-2009.title: Progression Models in Resistance Training for Healthy Adults
acsm-2009.support: For novice (untrained individuals with no RT experience or who have not trained for several years) training, it is recommended that loads correspond to a repetition range of an 8-12 repetition maximum (RM). The recommendation for training frequency is 2-3 d x wk(-1) for novice training, 3-4 d x wk(-1) for intermediate training, and 4-5 d x wk(-1) for advanced training.

mcdonald-beginning-1.title: Beginning Weight Training Part 1
mcdonald-beginning-1.support: Who counts as a beginner, how long the stage lasts, the signs it has ended, and the case for doing the least training that still produces progress.

mcdonald-beginning-2.title: Beginning Weight Training Part 2
mcdonald-beginning-2.support: What the beginner months are for: balanced base, learning the lifts, finding exercises that suit, slow joint and tendon adaptation, work capacity and tolerance for effort.

currier-2026.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
currier-2026.support: We synthesized data from 137 systematic reviews (>30,000 participants). Few RT prescription (RTx) variables affected primary adaptations. However, voluntary strength was enhanced by lifting heavier loads (>=80% one-repetition maximum), through a complete range of motion, for 2-3 sets, at the beginning of training sessions, and >=2 sessions/wk. Muscle hypertrophy was enhanced by higher volumes (>=10 sets/wk) and eccentric overload. Power was enhanced by moderate loads (30%-70% one-repetition maximum), low-to-moderate volume, Olympic-style weightlifting, and power RT (fast concentric phase).

rhea-2003.title: A Meta-analysis to Determine the Dose Response for Strength Development
rhea-2003.support: A meta-analysis of 140 studies with a total of 1433 effect sizes. Training with a mean intensity of 60% of one repetition maximum elicits maximal gains in untrained individuals, whereas 80% is most effective in those who are trained. Untrained participants experience maximal gains by training each muscle group 3 d.wk and trained individuals 2 d.wk. Four sets per muscle group elicited maximal gains in both trained and untrained individuals.

kubo-2010.title: Time Course of Changes in Muscle and Tendon Properties During Strength Training and Detraining
kubo-2010.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
kubo-2010.support: Eight subjects completed 3 months of isometric knee extension training. Training increased muscle strength and neural activation level by 29.6 and 7.3% after 2 months and by 40.5 and 8.9% after 3 months. Muscle CSA and tendon stiffness did not change until 2 months of training period, and afterward, the increases reached statistical significance at the end of training period.

bohm-2015.title: Human tendon adaptation in response to mechanical loading: a systematic review and meta-analysis of exercise intervention studies on healthy adults
bohm-2015.support: The review process yielded 27 studies with 37 separate interventions on either the Achilles or patellar tendon (264 participants). SMD was 0.70 for tendon stiffness. The subgroup analysis confirmed that stiffness adaptation significantly depends on loading intensity, but not on muscle contraction type. Although not significantly different, SMD was higher for interventions with longer duration (>=12 weeks).

steele-2022.title: Are Trainees Lifting Heavy Enough? Self-Selected Loads in Resistance Exercise: A Scoping Review and Exploratory Meta-analysis
steele-2022.support: CONCLUSIONS: Participants selected loads equal to an average of 53% of 1RM across exercises.

mcdonald-beginning-6.title: A Guide to Beginning Weight Training: Part 6
mcdonald-beginning-6.support: Rep-range progression, sizing weight jumps, the two-week definition of a stall, the 10 to 20% reset, when to change exercises and what the move to intermediate training looks like.

mcdonald-beginning-3.title: Beginning Weight Training Part 3
mcdonald-beginning-3.support: His beginner settings for load, sets, reps, weekly frequency and exercise choice, the objection to splits, and the practical trade-offs between free weights and machines.

ralston-2017.title: The Effect of Weekly Set Volume on Strength Gain: A Meta-Analysis
ralston-2017.support: Pre- versus post-training strength gains were greater with HWS compared with LWS [mean effect size (ES) 0.18; 95% CI 0.06-0.30; p = 0.003].

ralston-2018.title: Weekly Training Frequency Effects on Strength Gain: A Meta-Analysis
ralston-2018.support: When RT is volume-equated for combined multi-joint and isolation exercises, there is no significant effect of RT frequency on muscular strength gain. Volume-equated ... LF vs HF [mean ES 0.03 (95% CI -0.20-0.27); p = 0.78].

ramos-campo-2024.title: Efficacy of Split Versus Full-Body Resistance Training on Strength and Muscle Growth: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis
ramos-campo-2024.support: 14 studies (392 subjects) that compared Sp and FB routines in terms of strength adaptations and muscle growth were included.

mcdonald-beginning-4.title: Beginning Weight Training Part 4
mcdonald-beginning-4.support: How he introduced a machine routine over three sessions, his adjustments for powerlifting and physique beginners, and his reservations about 5x5 barbell plans.

haugen-2023.title: Effect of free-weight vs. machine-based strength training on maximal strength, hypertrophy and jump performance – a systematic review and meta-analysis
haugen-2023.journal: BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation
haugen-2023.support: Thirteen studies with a total sample of 1016 participants were included. Strength in free-weight tests increased significantly more with free-weight training than with machines, while strength in machine-based tests tended to increase more with machine training. No differences were detected in the direct comparison of strength, jump performance and muscle hypertrophy.

paoli-2017.title: Resistance Training with Single vs. Multi-joint Exercises at Equal Total Load Volume: Effects on Body Composition, Cardiorespiratory Fitness, and Muscle Strength
paoli-2017.support: Thirty-six participants; total work volume was equated; three times a week for 8 weeks. Both groups decreased body fat and increased fat free mass with no difference between them. Improvements in MJ group were higher than for SJ in VO2max (5.1 and 12.5%), bench press 1 RM (8.1 and 10.9%), knee extension 1 RM (12.4 and 18.9%) and squat 1 RM (8.3 and 13.8%).

mcdonald-beginning-5.title: A Guide to Beginning Weight Training: Part 5
mcdonald-beginning-5.support: How a beginner picks first weights from the light end, why body-weight formulas fail, and how few warm-up sets and how little stretching a new lifter needs.

chaves-2024.title: Effects of Resistance Training Overload Progression Protocols on Strength and Muscle Mass
chaves-2024.support: In conclusion, our findings indicate that the progression of overload through load or repetitions can be used to promote gains in strength and muscle hypertrophy in young men and women in the early stages of training.

mcdonald-health-fitness.title: Training for Health and Fitness Q&A
mcdonald-health-fitness.support: How little lifting general health needs, simple ways to vary reps after the first year, the place of occasional heavier sets and axial loading, and weekly layouts with cardio.

mcdonald-categories-7.title: Categories of Weight Training: Part 7
mcdonald-categories-7.support: Strength as the product of muscular and neural factors plus fixed leverage, how maximal strength is defined, and which goals need dedicated maximal strength work.

suchomel-2018.title: The Importance of Muscular Strength: Training Considerations
suchomel-2018.support: Strength is underpinned by a combination of morphological and neural factors including muscle cross-sectional area and architecture, musculotendinous stiffness, motor unit recruitment, rate coding, motor unit synchronization, and neuromuscular inhibition. While 2- to 5-min interset rest intervals may produce the greatest strength-power benefits, rest interval length may vary. Weaker athletes should focus on developing strength before emphasizing power-type training.

folland-2007.title: The Adaptations to Strength Training
folland-2007.support: The primary morphological adaptations involve an increase in the cross-sectional area of the whole muscle and individual muscle fibres. Changes in inter-muscular coordination appear critical. Adaptations in agonist muscle activation, as assessed by electromyography, tetanic stimulation and the twitch interpolation technique, suggest small, but significant increases.

mcdonald-categories-8.title: Categories of Weight Training: Part 8
mcdonald-categories-8.support: The 85 to 100% strength zone and its soft edges, and why grinding lifts allow fewer heavy days than fast lifts even in high-frequency systems.

peterson-2004.title: Maximizing Strength Development in Athletes: A Meta-Analysis to Determine the Dose-Response Relationship
peterson-2004.journal: The Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
peterson-2004.support: A meta-analysis of 37 studies with a total of 370 effect sizes. Effect size data demonstrate that maximal strength gains are elicited among athletes who train at a mean training intensity of 85% of 1 repetition maximum (1RM), 2 days per week, and with a mean training volume of 8 sets per muscle group.

suchomel-2016.title: The Importance of Muscular Strength in Athletic Performance
suchomel-2016.support: Greater muscular strength is strongly associated with improved force-time characteristics. Much research supports the notion that greater muscular strength can enhance the ability to perform general sport skills such as jumping, sprinting, and change of direction tasks. It appears that there may be no substitute for greater muscular strength.

mcdonald-categories-9.title: Categories of Weight Training: Part 9
mcdonald-categories-9.support: Strength volume: the limits of Prilepin's chart, the 3 to 5 sets of 3 to 5 reps rule, long rests and why only one or two lifts in a session can be trained heavy.

desalles-2009.title: Rest Interval between Sets in Strength Training
desalles-2009.support: In terms of acute responses, a key finding was that when training with loads between 50% and 90% of one repetition maximum, 3-5 minutes' rest between sets allowed for greater repetitions over multiple sets.

mcdonald-categories-10.title: Categories of Weight Training: Part 10
mcdonald-categories-10.support: Power as work over time, how fast force rises within the 0.1 to 0.2 second window sport allows, who needs power training, and the 30 to 70% load range for peak power.

mcdonald-categories-11.title: Categories of Weight Training: Part 11
mcdonald-categories-11.support: The force-velocity curve as a way to sort speed, power and strength work, and how a sport's implement and body size decide which part an athlete trains.

cormie-2011.title: Developing Maximal Neuromuscular Power
cormie-2011.support: A fundamental relationship exists between strength and power, which dictates that an individual cannot possess a high level of power without first being relatively strong. Ballistic, plyometric and weightlifting exercises can be used effectively as primary exercises within a power training programme. The use of ballistic exercises with loads ranging from 0% to 50% of one-repetition maximum (1RM) and/or weightlifting exercises performed with loads ranging from 50% to 90% of 1RM appears to be the most potent loading stimulus for improving maximal power in complex movements.

soriano-2015.title: The Optimal Load for Maximal Power Production During Lower-Body Resistance Exercises: A Meta-Analysis
soriano-2015.support: A total of 27 studies with 468 subjects. Moderate loads (from >30 to <70% of 1RM) appear to provide the optimal load for power production in the squat exercise. Lighter loads (<=30% of 1RM) showed the highest peak power production in the jump squat. Heavier loads (>=70% of 1RM) resulted in greater peak power production in the power clean and hang power clean.

soriano-2017.title: The Optimal Load for Maximal Power Production During Upper-Body Resistance Exercises: A Meta-Analysis
soriano-2017.support: A total of 11 studies with 434 subjects. Moderate loads (from >30 to <70 % of 1RM) appear to provide the optimal load for peak power and mean power in the bench press exercise. Lighter loads (<30 % of 1RM) appear to provide the highest mean and highest peak power production in the bench press throw exercise. However, a substantial heterogeneity was detected.

mcdonald-categories-12.title: Categories of Weight Training: Part 12
mcdonald-categories-12.support: Why lifts that begin and end at rest force the lifter to brake the bar, which makes them poor power exercises next to throws, jumps and Olympic lifts.

mcdonald-categories-13.title: Categories of Weight Training: Part 13
mcdonald-categories-13.support: Olympic lifts as power exercises and the time they take to learn; the hazards of bar throws and loaded jump squats; medicine balls, swings and jumps as the practical choice.

mcdonald-categories-14.title: Categories of Weight Training: Part 14
mcdonald-categories-14.support: Quality as the rule for power work: ending sets when speed drops, simple ways to measure output, the long warm-up fast work needs, and short sets with long rests.

mcdonald-categories-15.title: Categories of Weight Training: Part 15
mcdonald-categories-15.support: The 20 to 30% reduction rule for fast lifting, slow progression of power work, why easy jumps need no strength threshold, and ordering a session from fast, skilled work to fatiguing work.

behm-1993.title: Intended rather than actual movement velocity determines velocity-specific training response
behm-1993.support: Eight men and eight women trained 3 days/wk for 16 wk by doing attempted ballistic unilateral ankle dorsiflexions against resistance that either rendered the resultant contractions isometric (one limb) or allowed a relatively high-velocity movement (other limb). Training produced the same high-velocity-specific training response in both limbs. The results suggest that the principal stimuli for the high-velocity training response are the repeated attempts to perform ballistic contractions and the high rate of force development of the ensuing contraction.

seitz-2016.title: Factors Modulating Post-Activation Potentiation of Jump, Sprint, Throw, and Upper-Body Ballistic Performances: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis
seitz-2016.support: The analysis comprised 47 studies and 135 groups of participants for a total of 1954 participants. The PAP effect is small for jump (ES = 0.29), throw (ES = 0.26), and upper-body ballistic (ES = 0.23) performance activities, and moderate for sprint (ES = 0.51). A larger PAP effect is observed among stronger individuals and those with more experience in resistance training.

mcdonald-all-you-need.title: All You Need to Know About Training
mcdonald-all-you-need.support: His commentary on an elite sprint-cycling coach: coaches overcomplicate before they simplify, and after a missed target or a personal best on maximal work the session ends.

mcdonald-categories-1.title: Categories of Weight Training: Part 1
mcdonald-categories-1.support: The idea of overlapping training zones, and his account of high-rep, short-rest metabolic work: its loading, its uses, and why it should not replace heavy training on a diet.

hooper-2014.title: Effects of Fatigue From Resistance Training on Barbell Back Squat Biomechanics
hooper-2014.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
hooper-2014.support: Twelve men and 13 women with at least 6 months of resistance training experience performed a highly fatiguing resistance training workout; knee and hip angles were recorded throughout the 55 repetitions of the back squat. The technique changes that occur in high repetition sets do not favor optimal strength development and may increase the risk of injury.

mcdonald-categories-2.title: Categories of Weight Training: Part 2
mcdonald-categories-2.support: His reading of hypertrophy against hyperplasia, the sarcoplasmic growth debate, tension as the primary growth stimulus and the small role of damage, burn and hormone spikes.

jorgenson-2020.title: Identifying the Structural Adaptations that Drive the Mechanical Load-Induced Growth of Skeletal Muscle: A Scoping Review
jorgenson-2020.support: An increase in mechanical loading induces a growth response that is mediated, at least in part, by an increase in the cross-sectional area of the myofibers (i.e., myofiber hypertrophy). However, very little is known about the ultrastructural adaptations that drive this response.

roberts-2020-sarcoplasm.title: Sarcoplasmic Hypertrophy in Skeletal Muscle: A Scientific “Unicorn” or Resistance Training Adaptation?
roberts-2020-sarcoplasm.support: Select evidence suggests sarcoplasmic hypertrophy, or a disproportionate expansion of the sarcoplasm relative to myofibril protein accretion, coincides with muscle fiber or tissue growth during resistance training. There is also evidence to support other modes of hypertrophy including a proportional accretion of myofibril protein (conventional hypertrophy), or myofibril protein accretion preceding fiber or tissue growth (myofibril packing).

wackerhage-2019.title: Stimuli and sensors that initiate skeletal muscle hypertrophy following resistance exercise
wackerhage-2019.support: Mechanical signals are the prime hypertrophy stimuli candidates. While exercise-induced muscle damage is probably not essential for hypertrophy, it is still unclear whether and how such muscle damage could augment a hypertrophic response.

damas-2018.title: The development of skeletal muscle hypertrophy through resistance training: the role of muscle damage and muscle protein synthesis
damas-2018.support: Thus, we conclude that muscle damage is not the process that mediates or potentiates RT-induced muscle hypertrophy.

morton-2016.title: Neither load nor systemic hormones determine resistance training-mediated hypertrophy or strength gains in resistance-trained young men
morton-2016.support: Our data show that in resistance-trained individuals, load, when exercises are performed to volitional failure, does not dictate hypertrophy or, for the most part, strength gains.

mcdonald-categories-4.title: Categories of Weight Training Part 4
mcdonald-categories-4.support: Counting volume as sets, reps or tonnage and the weakness of each; his reps-per-muscle guideline and his reading of the Wernbom review.

wernbom-2007.title: The Influence of Frequency, Intensity, Volume and Mode of Strength Training on Whole Muscle Cross-Sectional Area in Humans
wernbom-2007.support: The purpose of this comprehensive review was to identify dose-response relationships for the development of muscle hypertrophy by calculating the magnitudes and rates of increases in muscle cross-sectional area induced by varying levels of frequency, intensity and volume. Tentative dose-response relationships for each variable are outlined, based on the available evidence.

mcdonald-categories-5.title: Categories of Weight Training: Part 5
mcdonald-categories-5.support: Halving direct work for muscles already trained by compound lifts, and fitting the choice of exercise to the rep range and to the lifter's build.

mcdonald-categories-6.title: Categories of Weight Training: Part 6
mcdonald-categories-6.support: Technical versus muscular failure, the occasional rep-out check on loading, one or two exercises per muscle, and the shared core of several named hypertrophy systems.

lopez-2021.title: Resistance Training Load Effects on Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Gain: Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis
lopez-2021.support: CONCLUSIONS: Although muscle hypertrophy improvements seem to be load independent, increases in muscle strength are superior in high-load RT programs.

mcdonald-categories-3.title: Categories of Weight Training: Part 3
mcdonald-categories-3.support: His point that growth training spans roughly 5 to 20 reps, that he can find no original research behind 8 to 12 as the growth range, and that low-rep growth work is slow and hard on joints.

pelland-2026.title: The Resistance Training Dose Response: Meta-Regressions Exploring the Effects of Weekly Volume and Frequency on Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Gains
pelland-2026.support: The posterior probability of the marginal slope exceeding zero for the effect of volume on both hypertrophy and strength was 100%, indicating that gains in muscle size and strength increase as volume increases.

halperin-2022.title: Accuracy in Predicting Repetitions to Task Failure in Resistance Exercise: A Scoping Review and Exploratory Meta-analysis
halperin-2022.support: RESULTS: The main multilevel meta-analysis model including all effects sizes (262 across 12 clusters) revealed that participants tended to underpredict the number of repetitions to task failure by 0.95 repetitions (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.17-1.73), but with considerable heterogeneity (Q(261) = 3060, p < 0.0001, I2 = 97.9%).

mcdonald-intensity-definition.title: What is Training Intensity?
mcdonald-intensity-definition.support: The case for describing a set by two separate intensities, load as a share of max and effort as closeness to failure, with further senses for neural, muscular and metabolic demand.

mcdonald-setting-intensity.title: Setting Exercise Intensity
mcdonald-setting-intensity.support: Why he sets lifting loads by a rep-max zone and reps in reserve for most people instead of a percentage of a tested max, and his cue for when to add weight.

helms-2016.title: Application of the Repetitions in Reserve-Based Rating of Perceived Exertion Scale for Resistance Training
helms-2016.support: A newly developed scale based on how many repetitions are remaining at the completion of a set may be a more precise tool. This approach adjusts loads automatically to match athlete capabilities on a set-to-set basis.

nuzzo-2024.title: Maximal Number of Repetitions at Percentages of the One Repetition Maximum: A Meta-Regression and Moderator Analysis of Sex, Age, Training Status, and Exercise
nuzzo-2024.support: A total of 952 repetitions-to-failure tests, completed by 7289 individuals in 452 groups from 269 studies. (Text: at 90% and 70% 1RM, ~5 and ~15 repetitions; bench press ~4, ~9, ~14 at 90, 80, 70% 1RM; SD about the point estimate 2.51 repetitions at 80% 1RM.)

zourdos-2016.title: Novel Resistance Training–Specific Rating of Perceived Exertion Scale Measuring Repetitions in Reserve
zourdos-2016.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
zourdos-2016.support: Our findings demonstrate an inverse relationship between average velocity and RPE/RIR.

mcdonald-warming-up.title: Warming Up For the Weight Room Part 1
mcdonald-warming-up.support: The jobs of a warm-up, a general warm-up ended at a light sweat, when stretching and activation drills are needed, short ramp-up sets scaled to the load, and optional heavy singles.

abad-2011.title: Combination of General and Specific Warm-Ups Improves Leg-Press One Repetition Maximum Compared With Specific Warm-Up in Trained Individuals
abad-2011.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
abad-2011.support: Thirteen participants were tested for leg-press 1RM under 2 warm-up conditions: a specific warm-up only, or the same after a 20-minute general warm-up on a stationary bicycle at 60% of HRmax. Strength values were on average 8.4% (p = 0.002) higher in the G + SWU compared with the SWU.

fradkin-2010.title: Effects of Warming-up on Physical Performance: A Systematic Review With Meta-analysis
fradkin-2010.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
fradkin-2010.support: Warm-up was shown to improve performance in 79% of the criterions examined.

souza-2024.title: Effect of warm-up protocols using lower and higher loads on multiple-set back squat volume-load
souza-2024.support: CONCLUSION: High or low equated-load CA used as warm-up strategies did not potentiate subsequent performance enhancement in multiple-set back squat exercise performed until muscle failure in comparison with usual warm-up.

kay-2012.title: Effect of Acute Static Stretch on Maximal Muscle Performance
kay-2012.support: 106 met the inclusion criteria. Clear evidence exists indicating that short-duration acute static stretch (<30 s) has no detrimental effect (pooled estimate = -1.1%), with overwhelming evidence that stretch durations of 30-45 s also imparted no significant effect (pooled estimate = -1.9%). A significant reduction is likely to occur with stretches >= 60 s.

behm-2016.title: Acute effects of muscle stretching on physical performance, range of motion, and injury incidence in healthy active individuals: a systematic review
behm-2016.support: A dose-response relationship illustrated greater performance deficits with ≥60 s (-4.6%) than with <60 s (-1.1%) SS per muscle group.

wiewelhove-2019.title: A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Foam Rolling on Performance and Recovery
wiewelhove-2019.support: Twenty-one studies. Pre-rolling resulted in a small improvement in sprint performance (+0.7%, g = 0.28) and flexibility (+4.0%, g = 0.34), whereas the effect on jump (-1.9%, g = 0.09) and strength performance (+1.8%, g = 0.12) was negligible.

mcdonald-5x5.title: A Look at the Classic 5X5 Program
mcdonald-5x5.support: Where five sets of five came from, why sets of five suit base strength, the difference between a ramp to one top set and five sets at one weight, and his rules for load and progression.

mcdonald-20-rep-squat.title: All About the 20 Rep Squat
mcdonald-20-rep-squat.support: How the breathing squat is performed, its origin as a finisher after heavy fives, his break-in and cycle-length advice, and his warning against 20-rep deadlifts and good mornings.

mcdonald-weider-principles.title: Some Less Well Known Weider Principles
mcdonald-weider-principles.support: A satirical piece; cited only for the background that Joe Weider's magazines relabelled existing gym methods as Weider Principles.

mcdonald-300-400-500.title: Bench Squat Deadlift for 300, 400, 500
mcdonald-300-400-500.support: The conditions attached to the 300, 400 and 500 lb targets: strict form, a lifter of about 90 kg, lifts done for reps, and why raw deadlifts exceed squats.

vandenhoek-2024.title: Normative data for the squat, bench press and deadlift exercises in powerlifting: Data from 809,986 competition entries
vandenhoek-2024.journal: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
vandenhoek-2024.support: Retrospective data from global drug-tested, unequipped powerlifting competitions were collated with 809,986 samples (571,650 males, 238,336 females). Relative strength was greatest for young adults (18-35 years; 90th percentile for squat [male: 2.83 x bodyweight, female: 2.26], bench press [male: 1.95, female: 1.35], deadlift [male: 3.25, female: 2.66]) before declining thereafter for all three exercises.

latella-2020.title: Long-Term Strength Adaptation: A 15-Year Analysis of Powerlifting Athletes
latella-2020.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
latella-2020.support: The rate of strength gain/day was assessed in 1897 PL athletes (F = 626, M = 1,271) over a 15-year period (2003-2018). The strongest males showed a lower rate of strength improvement (0.102 kg/d) compared with least strong males (0.211 kg/d), p = 0.010. The strongest males improve more slowly, possibly due to a ceiling effect.

williamson-2022.title: The performance and psychological effects of goal setting in sport: A systematic review and meta-analysis
williamson-2022.journal: International Review of Sport and Exercise Psychology
williamson-2022.support: Searches returned 17,841 articles, with 27 meeting eligibility criteria. Process goals had the largest effect on performance (d = 1.36) compared to performance goals (d = 0.44) and outcome goals (d = 0.09). Process goals also had large effects on self-efficacy (d = 1.11).

mcdonald-goal-process.title: Goal vs. Process Oriented Training: Part 1
mcdonald-goal-process.support: The contrast between athletes who judge themselves by results and those who judge by execution, the burnout and tension spiral of the first, and his preference for the second.

mcdonald-control.title: What You Can Control vs. What You Can't Control
mcdonald-control.support: His rule to acknowledge fixed factors such as leverage and trainability, use them only to shape the approach, and spend effort on training, recovery and diet.

mcdonald-coaching-yourself.title: Strategies for Coaching Yourself
mcdonald-coaching-yourself.support: Why self-coached lifters rationalise doing too much, and three checks: advise yourself as you would another lifter, treat doubt about one more set as a no, and halve the plan you wrote.

fisher-2022.title: The Role of Supervision in Resistance Training; an Exploratory Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
fisher-2022.journal: International Journal of Strength and Conditioning
fisher-2022.support: 12 studies were included in the review; 301 and 276 participants were in supervised and unsupervised groups, respectively. For strength there was a moderate effect favouring SUP (0.40 [95%CI = 0.06 to 0.74]). The main model for all body composition effects revealed a trivial standardised point estimate favouring SUP (0.07).

norton-2001.title: Morphological Evolution of Athletes Over the 20th Century
norton-2001.support: Sport is Darwinian in that only the 'fittest' reach the highest level of participation. Athletes in many sports have been getting taller and more massive over time; the rates of rise outstripping those of the secular trend. There are sports that demand a narrow range of morphological characteristics. In these sports the size of the most successful athletes over the century has remained constant.

mcdonald-look-like-athlete.title: Train Like an Athlete, Look Like an Athlete
mcdonald-look-like-athlete.support: His argument that there is no single athletic physique or training style, and that sports select body types far more than their training creates them.

mcdonald-success-clues.title: Success Leaves Clues
mcdonald-success-clues.support: A tongue-in-cheek piece whose serious point is that habits picked from champions are shared by the unsuccessful, and that the real common factor is a decade of consistent work plus talent.

balachandran-2022.title: Comparison of Power Training vs Traditional Strength Training on Physical Function in Older Adults
balachandran-2022.support: A total of 20 RCTs enrolling 566 community-living older adults (mean age 70.1 years). PT was associated with an improvement in physical function with low-certainty evidence in 13 RCTs (n = 383) (SMD, 0.30; 95% CI, 0.05-0.54). PT was associated with a modest improvement in physical function compared with traditional strength training in healthy, community-living older adults.

garber-2011.title: Quantity and Quality of Exercise for Developing and Maintaining Cardiorespiratory, Musculoskeletal, and Neuromotor Fitness in Apparently Healthy Adults
garber-2011.support: Educating adults about and screening for signs and symptoms of CHD and gradual progression of exercise intensity and volume may reduce the risks of exercise. Adults who are unable or unwilling to meet the exercise targets outlined here still can benefit from engaging in amounts of exercise less than recommended.

bull-2020.title: World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour
bull-2020.support: All adults should undertake 150-300 min of moderate-intensity, or 75-150 min of vigorous-intensity physical activity, or some equivalent combination, per week. The guidelines recommend regular muscle-strengthening activity for all age groups.

watson-2018.title: High-Intensity Resistance and Impact Training Improves Bone Mineral Density and Physical Function in Postmenopausal Women With Osteopenia and Osteoporosis: The LIFTMOR Randomized Controlled Trial
watson-2018.journal: Journal of Bone and Mineral Research
watson-2018.support: 101 postmenopausal women with low bone mass; 8 months of twice-weekly 30-minute supervised HiRIT (5 sets of 5 repetitions, >85% 1RM) versus home-based low-intensity exercise. LS BMD 2.9% vs -1.2%; only one adverse event reported in HiRIT (minor lower back spasm).

williams-2017.title: Comparison of Periodized and Non-Periodized Resistance Training on Maximal Strength: A Meta-Analysis
williams-2017.support: The cumulative results of 81 effects gathered from 18 studies ... indicated that the magnitude of improvement in 1RM following periodized resistance training was greater than non-periodized resistance training (ES = 0.43, 95% CI 0.27-0.58; P < 0.001).
